question: Under the Employment Act 1968, what is the minimum notice needed to terminate the service of an employee who has been employed for 2 years or more but less than 5 years, if the contract says nothing about notice?
answer: At least 2 weeks' notice is required, because without a contractual provision the notice period follows section 10(3).

This rule provides that, where an employee is wrongfully terminated (as opposed to dismissed with cause), the normal amount of damages he can claim is that which he would have been able to earn under his contract of employment, for the period it would take for his employer to lawfully terminate it. question: My employment contract doesn't say how much notice is needed to end it, and I have worked for the company for six years. What is the minimum notice either of us must give?
answer: At least 4 weeks' notice, the minimum for someone employed for 5 years or more; the same length applies to both employer and employee.

If the court applies the restriction in Braganza to the termination clause in this case, it would effectively be limiting such freedom. Nothing in Mr Choo's submissions satisfied us that there are sufficient reasons to alter so fundamental a premise of contract law in Singapore. Furthermore, in the case of employment contracts, the right to terminate with notice or pay in lieu of notice tends to cut both ways. This was, in fact, the case here. That, however, would seem to be a particularly unpalatable proposition in the field of employment law, where it is trite that employers cannot be compelled to hire or retain, but more importantly, that employees cannot be forced to work. We therefore suggest, albeit only in obiter , that the position advanced by Mr Choo was not an acceptable direction in which the law of contracts ought to be developed.

The second defendant set up an investigation team and found: (a) that there was no foul play; (b) that the husband did not have a good reason for going out onto the vessel's deck that night, though it did not take steps to rule out the possibility; and (c) that the husband had committed suicide, in light of messages he exchanged with the plaintiff showing that he had been troubled by financial, amongst other worries. question: Am I entitled to a day off every week, and does my employer have to pay me for that day?
answer: Every employee must be allowed one whole rest day each week, but it is without pay. It is Sunday or another day the employer determines.

The rest day must be Sunday or another day determined by the employer from time to time; an employee engaged in shift work may instead be given a continuous 30-hour period as the rest day. [CITE:2] If the employer determines the rest days, it must prepare a roster before the beginning of the month showing the appointed rest days. [CITE:2]

An employer generally cannot compel an employee to work on the rest day unless the nature of the work requires it to be carried on continuously through successive shifts, subject to statutory exceptions; in a dispute, the Commissioner of Labour decides whether that condition is met. [CITE:1]

If you work on the rest day, payment depends on who requested the work: [CITE:1]

- **At your own request:** if you work no more than half your normal hours, you receive half a day’s basic pay; if you work more than half but no more than your normal hours, you receive one day’s basic pay; if you exceed your normal hours, you receive one day’s basic pay plus at least 1.5 times your hourly basic rate for each excess hour or part-hour. - **At your employer’s request:** if you work no more than half your normal hours, you receive one day’s basic pay; if you work more than half but no more than your normal hours, you receive two days’ basic pay; if you exceed your normal hours, you receive two days’ basic pay plus at least 1.5 times your hourly basic rate for each excess hour or part-hour. “Normal hours of work” means the agreed usual hours of work, subject to the applicable statutory limits. [CITE:1]

A public holiday is a separate entitlement: if a public holiday falls on a rest day, the next working day following that rest day is a paid holiday. question: An employee has worked for an employer for 3 years under a contract that is silent on notice. Under the Employment Act 1968, what must the employer pay to end the contract immediately without giving notice?
answer: The employer must pay a sum equal to the salary at the gross rate of pay that would have accrued during the notice period, which for 2 to 5 years of service is 2 weeks.

question: If a public holiday falls on a Sunday, is another day given off instead?
answer: Yes. The next day after that Sunday that is not itself a public holiday is declared a public holiday in Singapore.

question: Under the Employment Claims Act 2016, what must a claimant do before lodging a claim against a respondent for a specified employment dispute?
answer: The claimant must first submit a mediation request to the Commissioner for every specified employment dispute the claim will cover.
evidence_quote: Before a claimant lodges a claim against a respondent, the claimant must submit to the Commissioner a mediation request
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, before lodging a claim, a claimant must submit to the Commissioner for Labour a mediation request relating to **every specified employment dispute** for which the claim will be lodged, in the prescribed manner and within the deadline applicable to that type of dispute [CITE:1][CITE:20].

If the dispute remains unresolved, an approved mediator must issue a claim referral certificate where the respondent was given reasonable notice but did not attend, no settlement was reached, or the mediator considers there is no reasonable prospect of settlement [CITE:6].

The claim is then lodged by filing it with the Registry, using the prescribed form or practice direction, and accompanying it with the claim referral certificate, any other required documents, and the prescribed court fee [CITE:2].

question: My former employer has appealed against the employment tribunal's order to pay me. Does the appeal stop me from enforcing the order in the meantime?
answer: No. An appeal against the tribunal's order does not stay its execution or enforcement unless a District Court or the General Division of the High Court orders otherwise.
evidence_quote: An appeal against an order made by a tribunal under section 22(1) does not operate as a stay of execution or enforcement of that order
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, **no—the appeal does not automatically stop enforcement of the employment tribunal’s order for the employer to pay you**. [CITE:1] [CITE:8]

Section 24(1) of the Employment Claims Act 2016 provides that an appeal against a tribunal order does not operate as a “stay of execution or enforcement” unless the District Court or the General Division of the High Court orders otherwise. [CITE:1]

Enforcement therefore continues unless such a stay is ordered; any stay may be subject to conditions, including payment of costs, payment into court, or the giving of security. [CITE:1] The General Division may order a stay only where the District Court has given permission to appeal and no stay application was made to any District Court. [CITE:1] [CITE:4]

question: Can a company in Singapore hire a foreign worker who does not hold a valid work pass?
answer: No. A person must not employ a foreign employee unless the employee has a valid work pass, and must employ them only in accordance with the pass conditions.
gold_citations: Employment of Foreign Manpower Act 1990, s 5
evidence_quote: A person must not employ a foreign employee unless the foreign employee has a valid work pass
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, no: a Singapore company generally cannot employ a foreign employee unless that employee has a valid work pass. [CITE:2]

The prohibition applies to both sides: an employer must not employ a foreign employee without a valid work pass, and the foreign employee must not be in an employer’s employment without one. [CITE:2] The company must also employ the worker in accordance with the conditions of the work pass. [CITE:2]

A valid work pass is tied to the specified employer and employee and to the specified trade, sector, occupation, or type of employment, unless the Controller has approved additional work. [CITE:4] It remains valid only for its stated period unless it is suspended, revoked, or cancelled. [CITE:4] Work passes are issued by the Controller, who may issue them with conditions or refuse the application. [CITE:5] [CITE:7]

An employer cannot rely simply on not knowing that the worker was a foreigner unless it proves due diligence, including checking the worker’s passport, identity document, or other travel document. [CITE:2] A first conviction for employing a foreign employee without a valid work pass may result in a fine of $5,000 to $30,000, imprisonment for up to 12 months, or both; a subsequent conviction against a company may result in a fine of $20,000 to $60,000. [CITE:2]

If the arrangement is genuinely self-employment rather than employment under a contract of service, section 10 separately prohibits a self-employed foreigner from carrying on that activity without a valid work pass. [CITE:7] [CITE:1] The Minister may also exempt particular persons or classes of persons from provisions of the Act by notification in the Gazette. [CITE:17]

sources.citation: Employment of Foreign Manpower Act 1990, s 5
sources.text: 5.—(1) A person must not employ a foreign employee unless the foreign employee has a valid work pass. answer: The person may appeal in writing to the Minister within 14 days of receiving notice of the decision, and the Minister's decision is final.

question: Do I need a licence to run a business that recruits and places workers in jobs?
answer: Yes. A person must not carry on an employment agency unless they hold a licence from the Commissioner.
evidence_quote: A person must not carry on an employment agency unless the person is the holder of a licence from the Commissioner
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, **yes, generally**. A person must hold a licence from the Commissioner for Employment Agencies to carry on an employment agency in Singapore. [CITE:2]

An “employment agency” includes an agency or registry carried on, or represented as intended to be carried on, in connection with the employment of persons in any capacity, whether or not it is conducted for gain or reward. [CITE:9]

The main exceptions include:

- An employer’s own recruitment registry established solely to recruit people for that employer’s own employment. [CITE:9]
- Work performed by employment agency personnel who are registered under section 12. [CITE:2] [CITE:11]
- An agency wholly maintained or managed by a Singapore Government department, or a person or agency exempted by the Minister by order. [CITE:13]

A person who carries on an employment agency without the required licence commits an offence punishable by a fine of up to $80,000, imprisonment for up to two years, or both; the corresponding limits for a second or subsequent conviction are $160,000 and four years. [CITE:2]

If the business recruits and places **seafarers**, it must also be authorised by the Director to operate a seafarer recruitment and placement service in Singapore, and the seafarer legislation expressly preserves the requirement to comply with the Employment Agencies Act 1958. [CITE:7]

Once licensed, the licensee must register employment agency personnel before allowing them to perform specified employment agency work. [CITE:11]

question: Under the Platform Workers Act 2024, what happens to the property of a platform work association when it is dissolved?
answer: The property immediately vests in the Official Receiver, who winds up the association's affairs and, after paying its debts and costs, pays any surplus as the Act directs, for example into the Workers' Fund if the Minister so directs.
evidence_quote: the property of the platform work association immediately vests in the Official Receiver
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, where a platform work association is dissolved under section 28(2), its property immediately vests in the Official Receiver. Section 28(2) applies when the association fails to register, its registration application is refused, or its registration is cancelled. [CITE:1] [CITE:4]

The Official Receiver must then wind up the association’s affairs. After paying the association’s debts and liabilities and the costs of winding up, any surplus assets must be dealt with as follows: [CITE:1]

question: Under the Platform Workers Act 2024, what is a "platform service"?
answer: A service specified in the First Schedule that is provided in Singapore through a digital or other platform by a platform operator that exercises management control over how its platform workers provide it.

As at 2026-11-06, the **Platform Workers Act 2024** defines a **“platform service”** as:

1. A service specified in the First Schedule;
2. Provided in Singapore through a digital platform or another platform; and
3. Provided by a platform operator that exercises management control over the service’s provision by one or more platform workers. [CITE:1]

The First Schedule specifies two types of platform services: **delivery services** and **ride-hail services**. [CITE:5]

A **delivery service** involves collecting goods or items from one or more places and delivering them to one or more other places. [CITE:5]

A **ride-hail service** is an on-demand passenger transport service or on-demand ride-booking service, of any type, using bookable vehicles. A bookable vehicle is a taxi or private-hire car hired or made available for hire as a whole with a driver to convey passengers. Taxi call-booking services and qualifying car-pooling arrangements are excluded. [CITE:5]

For these statutory purposes, a platform worker provides a platform service by performing one or more tasks relating to its provision by the platform operator. [CITE:1]

question: I am a woman about to give birth. How long can I be away from work in the usual arrangement around the birth?
answer: Under the default arrangement, she may be absent for the 4 weeks immediately before her confinement and the 8 weeks immediately after it; other agreed 12-week arrangements are also possible.

generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, the length of your maternity absence around the birth is governed by Part 9 of the Employment Act 1968 (EA), and for employees who meet the eligibility conditions in the Child Development Co-Savings Act 2001 (CDCA), by section 9 of that Act, which gives a more generous standard arrangement. [CITE:1][CITE:4]

## The usual arrangement: 16 weeks (4 weeks before + 12 weeks after)

If you satisfy section 9A of the CDCA, the standard option under section 9(1)(a) entitles you to be absent from work for 4 weeks immediately before your confinement and 12 weeks immediately after it, which is 16 weeks in total around the birth. [CITE:4][CITE:9]

Two alternative arrangements are also possible. [CITE:4]

- **One continuous agreed period of 16 weeks**, starting not earlier than 28 days before the day of your confinement and not later than the day of your confinement. [CITE:4]
- **An agreed first block of 8 weeks** starting within that same 28-day window, followed by one or more further agreed periods whose combined length equals 8 times your weekly index or 48 days, whichever is lower, all to be taken within 12 months beginning on the day of your confinement. [CITE:4]

## Who qualifies for the CDCA arrangements

Section 9A(1) requires that your confinement occurs (or the estimated delivery date is) on or after 1 January 2017, or for a stillborn child on or after 1 November 2021; that the child is a Singapore citizen at birth, or would have been for a stillborn child; and that you have served your employer for at least 3 months before the day of your confinement. [CITE:9]

If the child is not a Singapore citizen at birth but becomes one within 12 months of birth, section 9A(1A) applies with section 9(1A), under which the leave and payment periods are tied to the date the child becomes a citizen, and the agreed flexible period must begin on or after that date and end within the 12-month post-confinement period. [CITE:9][CITE:10][CITE:14][CITE:6]

## If the CDCA arrangements do not apply to you: the EA position

Under section 76(1) of the EA, the standard entitlement is 4 weeks immediately before confinement plus 8 weeks immediately after it, or 12 weeks in total. [CITE:1] You may instead take an agreed 12-week period starting within the 28-day window, or an agreed 8-week period followed by further agreed periods whose total length is worked out under the Fifth Schedule, or 24 days, whichever is lower, with all of it taken within 12 months beginning on the day of your confinement. [CITE:1] Under the Fifth Schedule, the calculation is 4 times your contractual work days per week where the pattern is constant, 4 times the total work days divided by the number of fixed weeks where there is a regular repeating pattern, or 4 times the average work days per week over the 3 weeks immediately preceding the earlier of the day of confinement and the first day of leave where there is no regular pattern, with half-day counting for any contractual working day of 5 hours or less. [CITE:8]

## Payment

Under section 76(1A) of the EA, payment at your gross rate of pay covers the 4 weeks before and the first 4 weeks after confinement under the first arrangement, the first 8 weeks of the 12-week agreed arrangement, and the 8-week agreed period under the flexible arrangement. [CITE:1] Section 9(1)(c) of the CDCA expressly requires payment at your gross rate of pay for the entire period of absence under the flexible arrangement, including the later agreed periods. [CITE:4] The excerpts provided do not spell out the provision that governs payment for every week of the 16-week CDCA arrangement, nor do they define "weekly index"; those points are not answered by these sources and would need to be checked in the full text of section 9 of the CDCA and section 76 of the EA on Singapore Statutes Online. [CITE:4][CITE:1]

## Notice, dismissal protection and related entitlements

- You must give your employer at least one week's notice before absenting, specifying your intended start date, and inform your employer of the confinement date as soon as practicable; failing to do so without sufficient cause reduces any payment to half. [CITE:5] For CDCA cases involving confinement on or after 1 April 2025, section 80 applies with modifications: no notice is required for absence under an agreed period under section 9(1), (1A) or (1B) or under an agreed flexible period, and the one-week notice becomes a prescribed period, or a shorter period agreed with your employer, for other absences. [CITE:20]
- It is unlawful for your employer to give you notice of dismissal during your absence, or on a day when the notice would expire during your absence. [CITE:7] A notice given without sufficient cause, or on grounds of redundancy or reorganisation, cannot deprive you of payments you would have received or would have become entitled to receive before your confinement in the circumstances set out in sections 84 and 84A. [CITE:3][CITE:2]
- If your employment ends before you have taken the flexible-period leave, you forfeit the untaken balance; if you resign before exercising any part of your maternity leave entitlement, you likewise forfeit the untaken balance and the related payment. [CITE:18][CITE:16]
- Employees with at least 3 months' service and a child below 7 years of age also have a separate entitlement to 2 days of paid childcare leave per relevant period, capped at 14 days per child, in addition to rest days, holidays, annual leave and sick leave. [CITE:17]

(2) An employee — (a) is not entitled to more than 14 days of childcare leave in respect of any child; and (b) must — (i) take his or her first entitlement of childcare leave of 2 days for a relevant period in that relevant period or the next succeeding relevant period; and (ii) then take his or her next and each subsequent entitlement of childcare leave of 2 days for a relevant period in the next succeeding relevant period and in each subsequent succeeding relevant period, respectively. (3) The childcare leave is in addition to the rest days, holidays, annual leave and sick leave to which an employee is entitled under sections 36, 88, 88A and 89, respectively. [55/2018] (4) An employer must grant, and an employee who is entitled to childcare leave must take, the entitlement of childcare leave of 2 days for a relevant period not later than the last day of that relevant period, and any employee who fails to take that leave by that day — (a) thereupon ceases to be entitled to that leave; and (b) is not entitled to any payment in lieu thereof. question: If a shop used an unfair practice when selling something to me, can I take the shop to court?
answer: Yes. A consumer who entered a consumer transaction involving an unfair practice may sue the supplier in a court of competent jurisdiction, unless the claim exceeds the prescribed limit.
evidence_quote: A consumer who has entered a consumer transaction involving an unfair practice may commence an action in a court of competent jurisdiction against the supplier
generated_answer:
**As at 2026-11-06, yes — in principle, a consumer may sue a shop in court for an unfair practice, subject to several statutory conditions.** Section 6(1) of the Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act 2003 (CPFTA) provides that a consumer who has entered a consumer transaction involving an unfair practice may commence an action in a court of competent jurisdiction against the supplier. [CITE:3]

## 1. Whether the Act applies to the transaction at all

Part 2 of the CPFTA, which deals with unfair practices, applies only if the supplier or the consumer is resident in Singapore, or the offer or acceptance relating to the consumer transaction is made in or is sent from Singapore. [CITE:20]

## 2. What counts as an "unfair practice"

Section 4 states that it is an unfair practice for a supplier, in relation to a consumer transaction, to do or say anything, or omit to do or say anything, if as a result a consumer might reasonably be deceived or misled, to make a false claim, to take advantage of a consumer if the supplier knows or ought reasonably to know that the consumer is not in a position to protect their own interests or is not reasonably able to understand the character, nature, language or effect of the transaction, or to do anything listed in the Second Schedule. [CITE:5]

Section 5 adds that an unfair practice may occur before, during or after a consumer transaction, may consist of a single act or omission, that the reasonableness of the person's actions in those circumstances must be considered, and that an act or omission by an employee or agent is also treated as the act or omission of the person if it occurred in the course of the employee's employment or the agent's exercise of powers or performance of duties within the scope of the agent's actual or apparent authority. [CITE:6]

Specific examples in the Second Schedule include: [CITE:8]

- Representing that goods or services have sponsorship, approval, performance characteristics, qualities, uses or benefits that they do not have. [CITE:8]
- Making a false or misleading representation concerning the need for any goods or services. [CITE:8]
- Representing that goods are of a particular standard, quality, grade, style, model, origin, weight, volume, length, capacity or method of manufacture if they are not. [CITE:8]
- Representing that goods are new or unused if they are not, or if they have deteriorated, been altered, reconditioned or reclaimed. [CITE:8]
- Representing that a price benefit or advantage exists where it does not. [CITE:8]
- Charging a price for goods or services substantially higher than an estimate provided to the consumer, except where the consumer expressly agreed to the higher price in advance. [CITE:8]
- Representing that a transaction involves or does not involve rights, remedies or obligations where that representation is deceptive or misleading. [CITE:8]
- Taking advantage of a consumer by including in an agreement terms or conditions that are harsh, oppressive or excessively one-sided so as to be unconscionable, or by exerting undue pressure. [CITE:8]

## 3. Which court can hear the claim, and monetary limits

- A Small Claims Tribunal has jurisdiction to hear and determine any action under section 6(1) insofar as it relates to an unfair practice involving a "relevant contract", which means a contract mentioned in paragraph 1(a) or (c) of the Schedule to the Small Claims Tribunals Act 1984, but excluding contracts relating to the sale of immovable property. [CITE:2]
- Section 6(2) limits the right to sue: it does not apply where the amount of the claim exceeds the prescribed limit, or where there is no claim for money and the remedy or relief sought is in respect of a subject matter whose value exceeds the prescribed limit. [CITE:3]
- The prescribed limit is $30,000 or any other amount that the Minister may prescribe by order in the Gazette. [CITE:3]
- For deciding whether an action under section 6(1) exceeds the District Court limit or the Magistrate's Court limit, the action is deemed to be a claim founded on contract. [CITE:2]
- If the amount of a claim exceeds the prescribed limit, the consumer may abandon the excess, after which the claim is treated as within the limit, no more than the limit may be recovered, and the court's order fully discharges all demands in respect of that cause of action. [CITE:3]
- Where a specified dispute resolution scheme was available to the consumer in respect of the dispute, the court must consider whether the consumer had sought to resolve the dispute through that scheme. [CITE:9]

## 4. What a court can order

In proceedings where a court other than a Small Claims Tribunal finds that a supplier has engaged in an unfair practice, the court may order restitution of any money, property or other consideration given or furnished by the consumer, award damages for loss or damage suffered as a result of the unfair practice, order specific performance, direct the supplier to repair goods or provide parts for goods, or vary the contract between the supplier and the consumer. [CITE:2]

Contract terms are also regulated by the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 (UCTA). [CITE:12] Section 3 UCTA applies where one contracting party deals as consumer or on the other's written standard terms of business, and provides that a contract term cannot exclude or restrict liability for breach, or entitle the party to render performance substantially different from what was reasonably expected or to render no performance at all, except so far as the term satisfies the requirement of reasonableness. [CITE:12] Section 12 UCTA sets out when a party "deals as consumer": the party neither makes the contract in the course of a business nor holds himself out as doing so, the other party does make the contract in the course of a business, and, for contracts governed by the law of sale of goods or hire-purchase, the goods are of a type ordinarily supplied for private use or consumption; on a sale by auction or competitive tender the buyer is not regarded as dealing as consumer in any circumstances, and a party claiming not to deal as consumer must show that fact. [CITE:13]

In sale and hire-purchase contracts, liability for the seller's implied obligations as to title, conformity with description or sample, and quality or fitness for a particular purpose cannot be excluded or restricted by a contract term against a person dealing as consumer. [CITE:10] For other contracts under which goods pass, corresponding liability for correspondence with description or sample and for quality or fitness for a particular purpose cannot be excluded against a consumer. [CITE:15] Liability for loss or damage arising from defective goods in consumer use that results from negligence cannot be excluded or restricted by a contract term or notice contained in or operating by reference to a guarantee of the goods. [CITE:16] A term making a consumer indemnify another person for liability that may be incurred for negligence or breach of contract is unenforceable against the consumer except so far as it satisfies the requirement of reasonableness. [CITE:19]

## 5. Time limits

No action under section 6 may be commenced later than 2 years after the later of the date of the occurrence of the last material event on which the action is based, or the earliest date on which the consumer had knowledge that the supplier had engaged in the unfair practice. [CITE:4]

question: Under the Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act 2003, what is the time limit for a consumer to start an action over an unfair practice?
answer: The action must be started within 2 years after the last material event it is based on, or after the earliest date the consumer knew the supplier had engaged in the unfair practice.

generated_answer:
**As at 2026-11-06, under the Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act 2003 (the "Act"), a consumer must start an unfair-practice action within two years.** [CITE:1] The provisions quoted in the sources are from the consolidated version in force from 9 March 2025, and the published copy itself directs readers to check Singapore Statutes Online for the latest version. [CITE:1]

## 1. The main time limit: two years

Section 6(1) allows a consumer who has entered a consumer transaction involving an unfair practice to commence an action in a court of competent jurisdiction against the supplier. [CITE:2] Section 12(1) provides that no such action may be commenced later than **two years** after whichever of these two dates is **later**: [CITE:1]

- **(a) the date of the occurrence of the last material event** on which the action is based; or [CITE:1]
- **(b) the earliest date on which the consumer had knowledge** that the supplier had engaged in the unfair practice to which the action relates. [CITE:1]

Because the test is "whichever occurs later", the two-year period can run from the date of knowledge even where that is later than the last material event, and vice versa. [CITE:1]

## 2. What "knowledge" means for this purpose

- For unfair practices under section 4(a) (deceiving or misleading a consumer) or 4(b) (making a false claim), and for any representation, act or omission that is false, deceptive or misleading, the consumer must know that the representation, act or omission was false, deceptive or misleading. [CITE:1]
- For unfair practices under section 4(c) (taking advantage of a consumer) or involving taking advantage of the consumer, the consumer must know that the supplier had taken advantage of the consumer. [CITE:1]
- It is irrelevant whether the consumer knew, as a matter of law, that the representation, act or omission amounted to an unfair practice; only factual knowledge matters for this limb. [CITE:1]
- Knowledge is not limited to actual knowledge: it includes knowledge the consumer might reasonably have been expected to acquire from facts observable or ascertainable by the consumer, or ascertainable with the help of appropriate expert advice that it would be reasonable to seek. [CITE:1] Section 12(8) also addresses the position where a fact is ascertainable only with expert advice, but the text of that subsection is cut off in the source provided. [CITE:1]

## 3. Court and monetary limit

- For an action under section 6(1), the prescribed limit on the amount of the claim is **$30,000**, unless the Minister prescribes another amount by order in the Gazette. [CITE:2]
- If the claim exceeds that limit, the consumer may abandon the excess, after which the claim is treated as within the limit, no more than the limit may be recovered in that action, and the court's order fully discharges all demands in respect of that cause of action. [CITE:2]
- A Small Claims Tribunal has jurisdiction to hear any action under section 6(1) insofar as it relates to an unfair practice involving a "relevant contract", which is a contract of a type listed in the Schedule to the Small Claims Tribunals Act 1984, excluding contracts for the sale of immovable property. [CITE:5]

## 4. Disability

For an action under section 6, the Fourth Schedule modifies section 24(1) of the Limitation Act 1959 so that, if the consumer was under a disability when the limitation period began to run, the action may be brought any time before the expiry of one year after the date the consumer ceased to be under the disability or died, whichever event first occurred, even if the limitation period has already expired. [CITE:4] Sections 24A, 24B and 24C of the Limitation Act 1959 do not apply to actions under the Act. [CITE:4]

## 5. Related but different time limits

The same section sets separate periods for other proceedings, which do not govern a consumer's own section 6 action: [CITE:1]

- Actions under section 8(6), (7) or (8) on a voluntary compliance agreement: one year after the date of failure to comply with the undertaking sought to be enforced. [CITE:1]
- Actions by the Commission under section 9 (declarations and injunctions): two years, running from the later of the last material event or the earliest date the consumer knew of the alleged unfair practice, in the terms described above. [CITE:1]
- Actions by the Commission under section 10 (injunctions against persons who knowingly abet, aid, permit or procure an unfair practice): two years after the last material event. [CITE:1]
- Actions under regulations made under section 11 (cancellation of certain contracts): one year after the date of cancellation of the contract. [CITE:1]

The underlying unfair practices that can ground an action are those in section 4: deceiving or misleading a consumer, making a false claim, taking advantage of a consumer in the circumstances stated there, and the specific practices listed in the Second Schedule, which include false or misleading representations about the need for goods or services, representing that a price benefit exists where it does not, charging a price substantially higher than an estimate without the consumer's prior express agreement, unconscionable terms, and omitting or concealing material facts. question: I asked the seller to fix a faulty product I bought. Who has to pay for the repair, and how quickly must it be done?
answer: The seller must repair or replace the goods within a reasonable time without significant inconvenience to the buyer, and must bear the necessary costs, including labour, materials and postage.

In Burdis v Livsey , the English Court of Appeal upheld the plaintiff's claim for damages for repairs despite the fact that she did not pay for the repairs and was under no legal obligation to do so as the credit repair agreement was unenforceable. The plaintiff's car was damaged in a road accident caused by the defendant's negligence. Rather than pay for repairs and wait for recompense from the defendant's insurers, the plaintiff entered into a credit repair agreement with Accident Assistance Limited ("AAL"). Under this agreement, AAL paid for the repairs upfront and took responsibility for securing ultimate payment (plus interest) from the defendant's insurer. Where an architect or engineer has caused damage to the property of another through his past negligence or breach of statutory duty, his liability lies in damages if at all. He cannot be ordered personally to repair or make good what he has damaged, any more than a surgeon, who has caused injury to a patient through negligent surgery, will be ordered to remedy that injury by operating on that injured person. Even where non-repair may result in further damage to the wronged party's property, the tortfeasor will not be ordered to undertake the repair of such property himself. Take the example of a car that is dented in an accident, and which may rust, allow the ingress of water and cause damage to other parts of the car if not repaired. The person who negligently caused the accident will not be ordered to repair the dent. Indeed, on ordinary principles, the wronged party must mitigate his loss by repairing damaged and deteriorating parts of his own property promptly. If he does not do so he would not be able to recover compensation for the reasonably avoidable further loss. question: Under the Hire-Purchase Act 1969, how can a hirer complete the purchase of the goods early?
answer: By giving the owner written notice of the intention and, on or before the day specified in the notice, paying or tendering the net balance due under the agreement.

**As at 2026-11-06, section 13 of the Hire-Purchase Act 1969 (Singapore) sets out the route by which a hirer under a regulated agreement may complete the purchase of the goods early.** [CITE:1]

## 1. While the agreement is still in force

- The hirer may give the owner **written notice of his intention** to complete the purchase, and on or before the day specified for that purpose in the notice, **pay or tender to the owner the net balance due under the agreement**. [CITE:1]
- This right may be exercised **at any time during the continuance of the agreement**. [CITE:1]
- The Act's own summary of hirer's rights in the Third Schedule likewise records that "you have the right to complete the agreement at any time". [CITE:12]

## 2. If the owner has already taken possession of the goods

- The same right is still available, but it must be exercised by payment to the owner **within 7 business days after the owner has served a notice in the form set out in the Fifth Schedule**, of the **net balance due together with the reasonable costs incurred by the owner incidental to his taking possession of the goods**, including storage, repair or maintenance costs. [CITE:1]
- The Fifth Schedule notice tells the hirer that, within 7 business days, the hirer may give notice of an intention to finalise the agreement and pay the balance due under the agreement and the cost of repossession; the form shows the owner's estimate of the balance due (total amount payable under the agreement less deposit and instalments paid), the cost of repossession, and the cost of storage, repair or maintenance. [CITE:7]
- The owner must serve that Fifth Schedule notice within 7 business days after taking possession of the goods; **if the notice is not served, the owner's rights under the regulated agreement cease and determine**. [CITE:15]
- Once that notice is served, the owner may not, without the hirer's written consent, sell or dispose of the goods or part with possession of them until 7 business days after service of the notice, or, if the hirer has already given notice under section 17(1)(a), until the time for payment or tender under that notice has expired, whichever is later. [CITE:6]

## 3. Effect of contrary contractual terms

- Any provision in the agreement excluding or restricting a right conferred on the hirer by the Act to determine a regulated agreement is void, and, except as the Act expressly provides otherwise, any provision excluding, modifying or restricting the operation of the Act's provisions is also void. [CITE:18]

question: I am paying for a car in instalments under a hire-purchase deal and want to stop. Can I end the arrangement by giving the car back?
answer: Yes. The hirer may end the hiring by returning the goods to the owner during ordinary business hours at the owner's usual place of business or the place stated in the agreement.

As at 2026-11-06, **yes**. Section 14 of the Hire-Purchase Act 1969 permits a hirer under a regulated agreement to terminate the hiring by returning the goods, although returning the car does not necessarily extinguish all liability under the agreement. [CITE:1]

### Returning the car

The statutory return procedure is:

- Return the car during ordinary business hours to the owner’s ordinary place of business or the place specified for returning goods in the agreement. [CITE:1]
- If the nature of the goods or the facilities at the relevant place make return there impracticable, the hirer may return them to a place agreed by both parties. [CITE:1]
- If the parties cannot agree on a place, the hirer may apply, with notice to the owner, to a Magistrate’s Court or District Court for an order fixing a reasonable return place; the court may also specify the termination date, subject to the car being returned. [CITE:1][CITE:20]

### Amount payable after return

The statutory notice to hirers states that a hirer unable to pay instalments may return the goods at their own expense and remains liable for an amount sufficient to cover the owner’s loss. [CITE:10]

After termination under section 14, the owner may recover the lesser of:

1. Any amount required to be paid in those circumstances under the agreement; or  
2. Any amount the owner could have recovered if it had taken possession of the goods when the hiring was terminated. [CITE:1]

Thus, returning the car ends the hiring but is not necessarily a payment-free cancellation. [CITE:1]

### Other statutory routes

A separate statutory route is early completion: the hirer may give written notice of the intention to complete the purchase and pay or tender the net balance by the specified date; after repossession, this must generally occur within seven business days after service of the prescribed notice, together with reasonable incidental possession costs. [CITE:7]

If the owner has already repossessed the car, it must serve the prescribed post-repossession notice on the hirer within seven business days; failure to do so causes the owner’s rights under the agreement to cease. [CITE:11] Within seven business days after service of that notice, the hirer may require redelivery, subject to section 18, or require the owner to sell the car to a cash buyer introduced by the hirer. [CITE:3] “Business day” means a day other than Saturday, Sunday or a public holiday. [CITE:20]

A contractual term cannot exclude the statutory termination right or impose greater liability on termination than the Act permits; such a term is void. [CITE:17]

question: Under the Supply of Goods Act 1982, what condition is implied when goods are hired out in the course of a business?
answer: There is an implied condition that the goods supplied under the hire contract are of satisfactory quality.

question: My luggage was stolen from my hotel. Is the amount the hotel has to pay me capped?
answer: Generally an innkeeper is not liable for more than $500, unless the loss was caused by the wilful act, default or neglect of the innkeeper or staff, or the property was deposited expressly for safe custody.
evidence_quote: to a greater amount than the sum of $500
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, **generally yes**. Under section 3 of the Innkeepers Act 1970, an innkeeper’s liability to a guest for stolen goods or property brought to the inn is capped at **$500**. [CITE:1]

The $500 cap does not apply where:

- the goods were stolen, lost or injured through the innkeeper’s or a servant’s wilful act, default or neglect; or
- the goods were deposited with the innkeeper or manager **expressly for safe custody**. [CITE:1]

The theft must fall within the first exception; section 3 does not say that every theft automatically removes the cap. [CITE:1]

For property expressly deposited for safe custody, the innkeeper or manager may require the guest to declare its value at the time of deposit and to place it in a fastened and sealed receptacle. [CITE:1] The innkeeper may refuse property with a declared value exceeding **$5,000**. [CITE:1] Liability for property accepted for safe custody cannot exceed its declared value. [CITE:1]

If the innkeeper or manager refuses to accept for safe custody property with a declared value not exceeding $5,000, or the guest cannot deposit it because of the innkeeper’s or manager’s default, the innkeeper cannot rely on the statutory limitation for that property. [CITE:2] The $500 figure is therefore a ceiling on the innkeeper’s liability, rather than an automatic payment of $500. [CITE:1]

Clause 9(a), for instance, states that Grassland "shall not be liable for any loss or damage to the passenger's personal belongings and luggage (kept in the luggage compartment of the coach) during the entire journey " [emphasis added]. Clause 18(d) excludes liability for "[t]raffic congestion, vehicle breakdown, obstruction of any public / private road or highway". I accept, however, that when these clauses are read in isolation, they are not unambiguous assumptions of responsibility to provide a transport service. The modern justification is not that it would be unfair to make a shipowner pay for all the damage he has caused: it is that a shipowner can obtain adequate insurance cover for third party claims if his insurers can calculate their maximum exposure with certainty. Victims generally benefit if the limits are set high enough and they can be sure that an insurer will pay their claim. In order for a shipowner to rely on the limitation of liability provided by s 136, he has the onus of proving that the loss or damage caused by the negligent navigation or management of his ship took place without his "actual fault or privity". The test of what amounts to "actual fault or privity" was set out by Lord Denning MR in The Eurysthenes [1976] 2 Lloyd's Rep 171 at 178—179 as follows: This was followed by a succession of Merchant Shipping Acts, all of them directed to limiting the responsibilities of the shipowner for the acts or defaults of his servants. He was not to be liable for acts done "without his fault or privity" beyond the value of the vessel. The object of these Acts was to limit his liability for his servants on the basis of respondeat superior, but to leave him fully liable for faults done by himself personally or with his privity … This historical survey shows to my mind that, when the old common lawyers spoke of a man being "privy" to something being done, or of an act being done "with his privity", they meant that he knew of it beforehand and concurred in it being done. If it was a wrongful act done by his servant, then he was liable for it if it was done "by his command or privity", that is, with his express authority or with his knowledge and concurrence.

The Court of Appeal restated (at [16] of Tan Swa Eng ) the well-accepted principle that: At common law, a person is an invitee if he is on private or public premises for a business purpose of material benefit to the occupier. This is usually referred to as a "common interest" as the invitee himself more often than not also has an economic interest in being on the premises. In contrast, licensees are those who have been given permission, whether express or otherwise, to enter premises and who are neither trespassers nor invitees. It was undisputed that the plaintiff in the present case was an invitee and not a licensee. The test of an occupier's duty of care vis-à-vis invitees may be found in the case of Indermaur v Dames (1866) LR 1 CP 274, and is based on the occupier taking reasonable care to prevent damage to the invitee from unusual danger. The test (at 288 of Indermaur v Dames ) was accepted and followed in Tan Swa Eng (see [17] to [19]). In short, an occupier is liable to an invitee for injuries and damage suffered only when all of the four elements below are satisfied (see The Law of Torts in Singapore (Gary Chan Kok Yew gen ed) (Academy Publishing, 2011) (" The Law of Torts in Singapore ") at para 10.014): (a) The occupier actually knew or ought to have known of the unusual danger ; (b) The danger was unusual to that class of plaintiffs having regard to the nature of the place and the knowledge of the invitee; (c) The danger was unknown to the plaintiff and the significance was not appreciated by the plaintiff; (d) The occupier failed to use reasonable care to prevent damage from occurring. [Limitation of liability] Section 136 of the Merchant Shipping Act provides, inter alia , that where a ship has, in the discharge of its cargo, caused damage to any property, the owner of the ship is entitled to limit his liability for such damage to an amount based on the tonnage of his ship and calculated in accordance with the formula provided in the section as long as such loss or damage was sustained "without his actual fault or privity". This section is the Singapore law enactment of the provisions of the International Convention Relating to the Limitation of the Liability of Owners of Seagoing Ships 1957 ("the 1957 Convention"), a treaty which over 50 state parties have ratified. The concept that a shipowner should be entitled to limit his liability when by reason of negligent management or navigation his ship collides with and damages another vessel or other property and/or causes loss of life or personal injury to passengers or crew or others was first codified in France in the 17th century. It was subsequently adopted by several other European countries. Limitation of a shipowner's liability for damage caused by the negligent management or navigation of his ship is an exception to the general rule that a person who negligently causes damage is responsible for the full financial consequences of the same provided such consequences are not too remote. However, this rule has been embodied in two international conventions in modern times, the 1957 Convention mentioned above, and the more recent treaty, the Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims 1976 ("the 1976 Convention"), and is apparently here to stay. Chorley & Giles' Shipping Law (8th Ed, 1987) states at pp 394—395 the justification for the rule: The convenience of the rule is responsible for its survival.

It would obviously be equally applicable to the condition of the premises and to activities being carried out on the premises. … [emphasis added] [(D) The United States] In the United States, the Supreme Court of California was the first to abolish, in 1968, the traditional tripartite distinction between trespassers, licensees and invitees. question: Under the Mercantile Law Amendment Act 1856, what is a surety who pays off the principal debtor's debt entitled to?
answer: To have assigned to him every judgment, specialty or other security held by the creditor for that debt, and to stand in the creditor's place and use all the creditor's remedies.
evidence_quote: shall be entitled to stand in the place of the creditor
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, section 2 of the Mercantile Law Amendment Act 1856 provides that a surety who pays the debt or performs the duty for which the surety was liable is entitled to have assigned to the surety, or to a trustee for the surety, every judgment, specialty, or other security held by the creditor in respect of that debt or duty. [CITE:1]

The surety also stands in the creditor’s place and may use the creditor’s remedies and, where necessary and upon a proper indemnity, use the creditor’s name in proceedings against the principal debtor, co-surety, co-contractor, or co-debtor to obtain indemnification for the surety’s advances and loss. [CITE:1]

Payment or performance by the surety does not bar those proceedings, but recovery between co-sureties, co-contractors, or co-debtors is limited to the just proportion that the party from whom recovery is sought bears among them. [CITE:1]

However, Singapore’s Application of English Law Act 1993 lists only sections 3 and 5 of the 1856 Act as applied in Singapore. The provided materials therefore do not show section 2 as operative Singapore law, although it contains the entitlement described above. [CITE:4][CITE:3][CITE:1]

sources.text: 313.—(1) Where the applicant for a bankruptcy order is a secured creditor of the debtor, the applicant must in the application — (a) state that the applicant is willing, in the event of a bankruptcy order being made, to give up the security for the benefit of the other creditors of the bankrupt; or (b) give an estimate of the value of the security, in which case the applicant may to the extent of the balance of the debt due to the applicant, after deducting the value so estimated, be admitted as a creditor in the same manner as if the applicant were an unsecured creditor. (2) Where an applicant for a bankruptcy order who is a secured creditor of the debtor fails to disclose the applicant’s security in the application, the applicant is deemed to have given up the security for the benefit of the other creditors of the debtor and upon the making of a bankruptcy order — (a) the applicant is not entitled to enforce the security against the estate of the bankrupt or to retain any proceeds from the realisation of the security; and (b) the applicant must execute such document of release as is required by the Official Assignee or account and pay over to the Official Assignee all proceeds from any realisation of the security. (3) Where any secured creditor fails to execute any document of release as is required by the Official Assignee under subsection (2)(b), the Official Assignee may execute the document on behalf of the secured creditor, and the execution of the document by the Official Assignee has the same effect as the execution of that document by the secured creditor. (4) Any secured creditor who fails to account or pay over to the Official Assignee the proceeds from any realisation of the security under subsection (2)(b) shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding $15,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 3 years or to both. (2) A creditor must file the creditor’s proof of debt with the Official Assignee under this Part in such form and manner as may be prescribed. (3) The Official Assignee must, in accordance with such regulations as may be prescribed, admit or reject, in whole or in part, any proof of debt filed under this Part. (4) Any debtor or creditor who is dissatisfied with the Official Assignee’s decision under subsection (3) may, within such time and in such manner as may be prescribed, appeal to the Court against the decision. (5) The Court may, on hearing an appeal under subsection (4), confirm, reverse or vary the decision of the Official Assignee. sources.text: 282.—(1) A creditors’ meeting summoned under section 281 may, if the meeting thinks fit, by special resolution resolve to approve the proposed voluntary arrangement, whether with or without modification. (2) The creditors’ meeting must not approve the proposed voluntary arrangement with any modification unless the debtor has consented to such modification. (3) For the purpose of this section, a modification subject to which a proposed voluntary arrangement may be approved by a creditors’ meeting may confer the functions proposed to be conferred on the nominee on another person qualified to act as a nominee. (4) No modification under subsection (3) may alter the proposal to such an extent that it ceases to be a proposal for a voluntary arrangement by the debtor. (5) The creditors’ meeting must not approve any proposal or any modification to the proposal which affects the right of a secured creditor of the debtor to enforce the secured creditor’s security, except with the concurrence of the secured creditor. (6) The creditors’ meeting must not, without the concurrence of the preferential creditor in question, approve any proposal or any modification of the proposal under which — (a) any debt of the debtor, not being a preferential debt, is to be paid in priority to any preferential debt of the debtor; or (b) the priority of payment of any preferential debt of the debtor, in relation to any other preferential debt of the debtor, is not in accordance with section 352. (7) Every creditors’ meeting must be conducted in accordance with the prescribed regulations. (8) Any debtor who makes any false representation or commits any other fraud for the purpose of obtaining the approval of the debtor’s creditors to a proposal for a voluntary arrangement shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding $10,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 3 years or to both.

question: A dealer was holding goods with the owner's permission and sold them to me in the normal course of business. Is my purchase valid even though the owner never approved the sale?
answer: Yes. The sale is as valid as if the owner had expressly authorised it, provided the buyer acted in good faith without notice that the dealer lacked authority.
evidence_quote: shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be as valid as if he were expressly authorised by the owner of the goods to make the same
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, the purchase can be valid even though the owner never separately approved the sale, provided the dealer satisfies the requirements of section 2 of the Factors Act 1889. [CITE:1]

Those requirements are that the dealer is a **mercantile agent**, possessed the goods with the owner’s consent, made the sale in the ordinary course of the dealer’s mercantile business, and dealt with you in good faith without notice that the dealer lacked authority. The sale is then as valid as if the owner had expressly authorised it. [CITE:1]

Section 2 requires consent to the dealer’s **possession**, not separate approval of each sale; consent to possession is also presumed unless evidence shows otherwise. [CITE:1] If you knew or had notice that the dealer lacked authority, however, the statutory good-faith and no-notice requirements would not be met. [CITE:1]

The supplied provision does not define “mercantile agent”, so describing the seller as a “dealer” does not conclusively establish that this statutory category applies. [CITE:1] Outside this statutory route, the general rule is that a sale by someone who is not the owner and lacks the owner’s authority or consent gives the buyer no better title than the seller had, unless the owner’s conduct precludes denying the seller’s authority; section 21 expressly preserves the Factors Act provisions. [CITE:2]

question: Under the Sale of Goods Act 1979, a business sells goods to a buyer who examined them before contracting. Is the seller liable for defects that the examination ought to have revealed?
answer: No. Business sales carry an implied condition of satisfactory quality, but that condition does not extend to matters which the buyer's examination before the contract ought to reveal.

answer: No. A person cannot use a contract term or notice to exclude or restrict liability for death or personal injury resulting from negligence.

sources.text: An employer's duty to keep the workplace safe is a duty that is intended for the careful worker, it must contemplate dangers that lay in wait for the careless ones as well, but if a worker injures himself through his own carelessness, he must bear some responsibility for the mishap. The extent of his contribution depends on the facts, and the greater the carelessness the more responsibility he has to bear. Low level carelessness may include simple absent-mindedness or momentary inattention though this also depends on the activity in question. Recklessness will form the higher levels of contributory negligence, and this includes cases where pedestrians injure themselves when they dash across a road without looking, giving the motorist only a small chance of avoiding the accident. The degree of contributory negligence at the reckless level depends on the actor and the act, of course, but sometimes the circumstances may also ameliorate or aggravate the liability of the parties. In this case, the defendant had bought the machine as it was, making no alteration or modification to it. If an accident had happened because of an unauthorised modification to a machinery, the employer who had modified it has to bear a greater responsibility for any accident that is attributed to that modification. The case before me is slightly different. The accusation here is that the defendant ought to have modified the machinery to make it safer. We can see at once how that complicates the apportionment of the defendant's responsibility. The defendant bought the machine from an established manufacturer. Were it to modify the machine, it runs the risk of imposing a greater responsibility should the modification cause problems in the use of the machine, and ultimately, accidents.

Contributory negligence arises where a plaintiff has acted in a careless manner, failing to take reasonable care for his own personal safety in the circumstances, with the result that he contributes in part to his own injury. The Court of Appeal in Parno v SC Marine Pte Ltd [1999] 3 SLR(R) 377 ( " Parno " ) at [59] cited with approval the observation of Lord Denning MR in Froom v Butcher [1976] QB 286 at 291: Negligence depends on a breach of duty, whereas contributory negligence does not. Negligence is a man's carelessness in breach of duty to others. Contributory negligence is a man's carelessness in looking after his own safety. He is guilty of contributory negligence if he ought reasonably to have foreseen that, if he did not act as a reasonable prudent man, he might hurt himself. The defendant is thus not required to show that a claimant has breached a legal duty of care, as is necessary in a claim for negligence (Gary Chan Kok Yew, The Law of Torts in Singapore (Academy Publishing, 2011) (" The Law of Torts in Singapore ") at para 07.071). For convenient reference, I set out s 3(1) of the Contributory Negligence and Personal Injuries Act (Cap 54, 2002 Rev Ed) which provides as follows: Apportionment of liability in case of contributory negligence 3. —(1) Where any person suffers damage as the result partly of his own fault and partly of the fault of any other person or persons, a claim in respect of that damage shall not be defeated by reason of the fault of the person suffering the damage, but the damages recoverable in respect thereof shall be reduced to such extent as the court thinks just and equitable having regard to the claimant's share in the responsibility for the damage . [emphasis added]

I begin my analysis with the insuring clause which was in the widest terms as was to be expected in a public liability policy. The words have been in use for a very long time and certainly since I began in practice. This cover was expressed to be an indemnity to indemnify the insured against: All sums which the insured shall become legally liable to pay for compensation in respect of 1. Accidental bodily injury (including death or disease) to third parties 2. Accidental loss and/or damage to property belonging to third parties occurring within the Territorial Limits in connection with the Insured's trade or business during the Period of Insurance. Hydro Aquatic provided lifeguard and pool cleaning services and I found that both services fell within its trade or business as described in the policy. Accordingly, OAC became legally liable to pay compensation in respect of unfortunate incidents like the death in this case and the question was whether such liability was excluded. In my judgment, I could not agree with OAC that the words "any employee" in the FAT/F clause referred to employees of Hydro Aquatic. The phrase "or any employee" could not be read disjunctively. The exclusion covered two main groups: first, duly qualified members of the medical profession; and second, any employee or voluntary worker of any hospital or ambulance organisation. The plain and ordinary meaning which would have been given to the phrase by the contracting parties was that it referred to employees of any hospital or ambulance organisation and not to employees of Hydro Aquatic. That was also the meaning that would be given to the exclusion by people in the industry. Professional indemnity is usually taken outside public liability clauses because it is generally the case that doctors or other employees of hospitals are themselves covered by their own professional insurance and there is no need to cover them twice. I found OAC's suggested reading remarkable and one that made no commercial sense. Moreover, the clause was an exclusion clause and it was incumbent on OAC to make it clear that "any employee" meant "any employee of the Insured" rather than to dispute the clause at a later stage.

No doubt a lifeguard is trained in first aid. He might even be trained in the use of specialist equipment. He might even be skilled in their use and certified as such. But he is not a person with the characteristics that I have described above. Thus I could not accept that lifeguards could be regarded as professionals in the sense of the word as I have explained above, let alone in the context of an insurance exclusion clause. It went against commercial sense that a business would attempt to get policy cover that excluded liability for any of its staff on the ground that its staff were to be regarded as professionals. OAC was not able to provide any authority which said that lifeguards were to be regarded as professionals in this context. A second reason for my decision that Exclusion 8(a) did not apply to exclude liability was that it did not refer to death but merely injury, loss or damage. I compared this to the main insuring clause which I cited at [132] above and which referred to bodily injury including death or disease . I relied on the approach in construction that exclusion clauses should be construed strictly and if an insurer wished to provide that cover was excluded in certain circumstances it should have done so in clear words; if it did not, any ambiguity or lack of clarity would be resolved against it (see Singapore Telecommunications Limited v Starhub Cable Vision [2006] 2 SLR(R) 195 at [52].)

The provisions in the 1995 Regulations set out in [38] certainly do not apply to this case as the evidence before this court was that the premises were not a shipyard of Keppel but those of the second defendant. Further, there was no evidence that the plaintiff was working on a ship at the material time. The second defendant's defence in [11] that s 60(1)(a) of the Workplace Act precludes the plaintiff from suing is a misreading of the provision. What the subsection means is, a contravention of the Act does not automatically confer a right of action on a workman per se . A breach of the statutory provision must be the cause of his injury before a plaintiff can rely on the breach to found his cause of action (see Mohd bin Sapri v Soil-Build (Pte) Ltd and another appeal [1996] 2 SLR 505 ). Hence, s 60 of the Workplace Act goes on to say:- (2) Subsection (1) shall not affect the extent (if any) to which a breach of duty imposed under any written law is actionable. The defendant does not dispute that it owes a duty of care to the plaintiff as its employee, but claims that it did not breach its duty of care for the following reasons: (a) First, the space between the rollers of the machine, ie , the part that the plaintiff's arm got caught in, was not such a dangerous part of the machine that it needed to be fenced up. In fact, the machine was approved for use in Singapore when it was acquired in 2006. The space between the rollers was not an area that the plaintiff would ordinarily come into contact with when he discharges his primary duties. (b) Second, such fencing was unnecessary given the availability of the power-off switch in close proximity to where the plaintiff was standing. This was a separate safety feature on the machine. The defendant's counsel further submits that if it is found to have breached its duty of care to the plaintiff, damages owing to the plaintiff should be apportioned owing to the plaintiff's contributory negligence. Counsel argues that the conduct of the plaintiff in attempting to dislodge the cans with his bare arm, before powering down the machine, created a significant risk of injury that could easily have been avoided. Counsel submits that it should pay only 10% of the total damages. The plaintiff's primary position on contributory negligence is that he was not contributorily negligent at all. In the alternative, his counsel submits that a minimal figure of 10% liability ( ie , to receive 90% of the damages) is appropriate should the court find the plaintiff to be contributorily negligent. The plaintiff submits that he was not properly trained to operate the machine, and that he was merely following a common practice adopted by his colleagues in using his hand to dislodge the can while the machine continued to run. In my judgment, the defendant is liable to the plaintiff for breaching its duty of care in not having sufficient fencing to stop workers reaching into the rollers, but I also accept that the plaintiff was partly responsible for the injury. I find that the plaintiff was contributorily negligent to the extent of 50%.

The difference between Bottomley and the present case is plain. Bottomley concerned an independent contractor in respect of which proper checks would have revealed to be (a) manifestly unsuitable for the task assigned and (b) led to the cancellation of the event or at least led the cricket club to insist that a safety plan be furnished. question: Two companies signed a contract that names me and says a term is for my benefit. Can I enforce that term even though I did not sign the contract?
answer: Yes, generally. A non-party may enforce a term that purports to confer a benefit on them if they are expressly identified, unless the contract shows the parties did not intend it to be enforceable by them.

Prakash J refused to extend the Interfoto Principle to signed contracts and held that the principle only applied to cases in which there was no signed contract ( Press Automation Technology at [39] and [40]). In my view, this position holds true even for contracts between businesses and consumers. It is telling that Prakash J declined to follow the Canadian case, Tilden Rent-A-Car Co v Clendenning [1978] 83 DLR 3d 400. In the context of a business-consumer contract, the Canadian court held that a signature can only be relied on as manifesting assent to a document when it is reasonable for the party relying on the signed document to believe that the signor really did assent to its contents. This does not represent the law in Singapore. Prakash J's holding and analysis at [39] and [40] of Press Automation Technology were endorsed by the Court of Appeal in Bintai at [61]. I am guided by the Court of Appeal's endorsement of Prakash J's reasons, two of which bear highlighting. First, as Prakash J cautioned, "[c]ontracting parties must have a care for their own legal positions by ascertaining what terms are to be part of a contract before signing it" ( Press Automation Technology at [40]). Second, she cited Hobhouse LJ's remark in AEG (UK) Ltd v Logic Resource Limited [1996] CLC 265 that recourse against onerous terms is already statutorily provided for in the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 (c 50) (UK). Therefore, it is no longer necessary to introduce additional strict criteria to prevent particular terms from being incorporated into a contract. Third, and in addition to Prakash J's views, it would result in unacceptable levels of uncertainty if signatories to a contract were allowed to disclaim terms which they find to be onerous or unreasonable. In these premises, I see no practical need to extend the Interfoto Principle to signed contracts.

It is well established that terms are not readily implied in law. Once a term has been implied in law, the term will be implied in all future contracts of that particular type. This can be distinguished from a term that is implied in fact, in which case the term only applies to the particular contract and parties. It behoves the court to approach terms implied in law with much care and circumspection, because a term that is implied in law establishes a precedent for similar cases in the future for all contracts of that particular type: see Forefront Medical Technology (Pte) Ltd v Modern-Pak Pte Ltd [2006] 1 SLR(R) 927 at [42]—[44]. Indeed, it has been said that the touchstone for implying a term in the contract is necessity and not merely reasonableness: see Hugh Beale gen ed, Chitty on Contract vol 1 (Sweet & Maxwell, 31st Ed, 2012) at para 13-010. To succeed in its position that the term should be implied in law, the Defendant needs to either show that there is a statutory provision which states that the term is to be implied, or there is some relevant custom and usage that requires the term to be implied: see The Law of Contract in Singapore at paras 06.076-06.090. However, in the present case, no independent evidence was led on the existence of any statute, custom or usage in respect of this term that the Defendant is urging the court to imply. Quite apart from the absence of proof, the Plaintiff rightly submits that the implication of such a term is inconsistent with the express terms of the OSTA 2012. The OSTA 2012 sets out in great detail the terms and conditions governing the contractual relationship between the Plaintiff and the Defendant. As discussed earlier, this includes Clause 23.1 under which the Defendant is held liable for trades even if they were executed by a third party , but with the consent and/or authority (express, implied or otherwise) and/or knowledge of the Defendant. There is thus no need for the Defendant's express authorisation, instruction and/or consent.

question: Under the Copyright Act 2021, when does copyright expire in an authorial work first published within 50 years after it was made, where the author is identified?
answer: It expires 70 years after the end of the year in which the author dies, provided the author is identified within 70 years after the end of the year of first publication.
evidence_quote: 70 years after the end of the year in which the author dies
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, where an authorial work is first published within 50 years after the end of the year in which the work was made and the author is identified, any copyright in the work expires **70 years after the end of the year in which the author dies** [CITE:1].

## The main rule and its conditions

- Section 114(1)(a) applies the death-based rule only where the author is identified within 70 years after the end of the year in which the work is first published; in that case copyright expires 70 years after the end of the year in which the author dies [CITE:1].
- If the author is not identified within that window, the alternative rule applies and copyright expires 70 years after the end of the year in which the work was first published [CITE:1].
- Because the period is measured from the end of the year of death, the copyright runs to the end of the 70th year following the year in which the author died, rather than to the date of death itself [CITE:1].

## What "identified author" means

- An authorial work has an identified author if the identity of the author is generally known or can reasonably be ascertained [CITE:9].
- For a work of joint authorship, it is enough that the identity of at least one of the joint authors is generally known or can reasonably be ascertained [CITE:9].
- An author whose pseudonym is generally known is not treated as having an identity that is generally known [CITE:9].
- For the purposes of sections 114 and 115, a reference to the death of the author in a work of joint authorship means the death of the last surviving identified author [CITE:10].

## Publication and subsistence conditions

- Section 114 is expressly subject to section 110(1)(b), which provides for copyright in a published authorial work to expire at first publication if the conditions for subsistence are not met [CITE:1].
- Under section 110(1), where copyright subsisted immediately before first publication, it continues to subsist only if either the author was a qualified individual when the work was first published (or died before first publication but was a qualified individual immediately before death), or the work was first published in Singapore, by or under the direction or control of the Government, or on or after 10 April 1987 by or under the direction or control of a prescribed international organisation [CITE:3].
- For acts done before 21 November 2021, sections 53 to 58 do not apply for deciding whether a work was published or whether a publication was the first publication; instead section 24 of the 1987 Act applies instead, as modified where applicable [CITE:19].

## Transitional rules that can displace section 114

- For a literary, dramatic or musical work or an engraving where the author was identified on or before 31 December 2022, died before 21 November 2021, and the work was first made available to the public after the author's death and on or before 31 December 2022, copyright expires 70 years after the end of the year in which the work was first made available to the public [CITE:2].
- "Made available to the public" is broader than publication: it includes public performance, communication to the public, publication, public exhibition of artistic works, construction of a building, and offering or exposing records of the work to the public, and unauthorised acts must be ignored in deciding the question [CITE:10].
- Section 115 is also subject to section 110(1)(b) on expiry of copyright upon publication [CITE:2].
- For a photograph taken before 10 April 1987, sections 114 and 115 do not apply, and copyright under Part 3 expires 70 years after the end of the year in which the photograph was taken, subject to any earlier expiration [CITE:13].
- For an authorial work first published before 10 April 1987 but made on or after 1 July 1912, Part 3 confers no copyright unless copyright subsisted in the work under the 1911 Act immediately before 10 April 1987 [CITE:5].
- Copyright that had already expired before 21 November 2021 under the 1987 Act is not revived or extended by Part 3, and the same applies to copyright that had expired before 1 July 2004 [CITE:6] [CITE:7].
- For an authorial work made before 10 April 1987 where the author was the first owner of copyright, the reversionary interest expectant on the expiry of 25 years after the author's death devolves, despite any contrary agreement, to the author's legal personal representative as part of the author's estate [CITE:8].

## Moral rights

- Moral rights apply only for the period during which copyright subsists in the work, and only in relation to the whole or a substantial part of the work [CITE:16].

The consolidated text of the provisions quoted above is stated to be the version in force from 9 March 2025, and the source directs readers to check Singapore Statutes Online for the latest version [CITE:1].
