question: I wrote a report as part of my job as a salaried employee. Who first owns the copyright in it, me or my employer?
answer: For works made in the course of a contract of service, the employer is the first owner of the copyright, subject to a special rule for some works made for periodicals.
evidence_quote: Subject to subsection (4), the employer is the first owner of any copyright in the relevant work
generated_answer:
**As at 2026-11-06, on the facts you describe — a report you wrote in the course of your employment as a salaried employee — your employer is generally the first owner of copyright in the report, unless a written agreement between you and the employer provides otherwise.** [CITE:1]

### Why the employer is normally the first owner

Assuming the report is an "authorial work" (the category of works to which the subsistence provisions in sections 109 and 110 apply), section 134 governs because it applies where an employee makes an authorial work in the course of a contract of service. [CITE:1] [CITE:7] [CITE:11] Under section 134(3), and subject to subsections (4) and (5), the employer is the first owner of any copyright in the relevant work. [CITE:1] The general default in section 133, under which the author is first owner of an authorial work, does not govern here, because section 134(2) provides that the first owner of an employment-made work is determined under section 134 and not section 133. [CITE:2] [CITE:1] In statutory terms, the first owner is the copyright owner and the "rights owner" for that work, and a copyright owner's exclusive rights are rights to exclude others rather than positive rights to carry out the acts themselves. [CITE:10] [CITE:14]

### Two exceptions that could change the position

1. **Contrary intention in an agreement.** Section 134(5) makes subsections (3) and (4) subject to any contrary intention in any written agreement made between employer and employee on or after 21 November 2021, or in any agreement made between them before that date. [CITE:1] A written employment contract or other signed agreement assigning the copyright to you would therefore displace the employer-ownership rule. [CITE:1]

2. **Publication in a periodical.** If your employer is the proprietor of a periodical (a newspaper, magazine or similar periodical, including an online periodical) and the report is a literary, dramatic or artistic work made for publication in that periodical, then for work made on or after 10 April 1987 the employer owns copyright only to the extent it relates to publishing the work in any periodical or making a copy for that purpose, and you are otherwise the first owner. [CITE:1]

### What does not alter the analysis

- **Commissioned works.** Section 135 covers certain pre-21 November 2021 commissions, but it applies only where the commissioned work was not done in the course of a contract of service, so it does not govern a report made in the course of your employment. [CITE:4]
- **Government as employer.** If your employer is the Government, section 136 makes the Government the first owner of copyright in, among other categories, an unpublished authorial work made by or under the direction or control of the Government. [CITE:5]

### Two further points

- **Employment status is assessed on substance, not labels.** Section 134 applies only where the work is made in the course of a contract of service. [CITE:1] In *Writers Studio Pte Ltd v Chin Kwok Yung*, the General Division of the High Court held that the employee–employer question is informed by the totality of the factual matrix and the contractual relationship, and that using the word "salary" instead of "remuneration" was not indicative of an employee–employer relationship. [CITE:16]
- **Moral rights.** Where an authorial work is made in the course of the author's employment and the employer is the first owner of copyright, the right to be identified under section 371 does not apply to that work. [CITE:3]

These ownership rules presuppose that copyright subsists in the report at all: for an unpublished authorial work, copyright subsists only if the work is original and, ordinarily, the author is a qualified individual when the work is made, and the provided sections do not reproduce the definition of "qualified individual". [CITE:11]

question: Under the Patents Act 1994, when is an invention taken to be new?
answer: An invention is new if it does not form part of the state of the art, meaning matter made available to the public anywhere before the invention's priority date.

question: Once a patent is granted for my invention, how long does it stay in force?
answer: It continues in force until the end of 20 years from the date the patent application was filed, provided the renewal fees are paid.

As at 2026-11-06, under Singapore’s Patents Act 1994, a patent generally remains in force until the end of the **20-year period beginning from the date its application was filed**, or from another date prescribed by law. [CITE:1]

The patent takes effect on the date the certificate of grant is issued, but the 20-year term is not calculated from the grant date. [CITE:1]

Renewal fees must be paid. If a renewal fee is not paid, the patent ceases to have effect at the end of the prescribed payment period; payment of the renewal fee and any prescribed additional fee during a further grace period can treat the patent as if it never expired for the purposes stated in the Act. [CITE:1]

The term may be extended under section 36A in defined circumstances, including certain unreasonable delays by the Registrar, specified delays involving corresponding or related national-phase patents, and certain pharmaceutical active-ingredient cases involving the first marketing approval of a pharmaceutical product. [CITE:4] An extension application must satisfy the prescribed filing period, form, manner, fee, and document requirements. [CITE:6]

A patent that lapsed because renewal fees were unpaid may be restored within the prescribed period if the Registrar is satisfied that the failure to pay was unintentional and the required unpaid fees and additional fee are paid, subject to any conditions imposed by the Registrar. [CITE:9]

A special transitional rule applies to certain patents registered from the United Kingdom: their term runs from the date of the UK patent, remains 20 years from that date, and continues only so long as the patent was not revoked in the United Kingdom before 17 October 2001, subject to the Act and prescribed modifications. question: I came up with an invention while doing my normal duties at work. As between me and my employer, who owns it?
answer: The invention is taken to belong to the employer if it was made in the course of the employee's normal or specifically assigned duties and an invention might reasonably be expected to result from them.
evidence_quote: is taken to belong to the employee’s employer for the purposes of this Act and all other purposes
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, under the supplied consolidated text of the Patents Act 1994, your employer owns the invention, as between you and the employer, if you made it in the course of your normal duties and the circumstances were such that the invention might reasonably have been expected from carrying out those duties. [CITE:1]

Making the invention during normal duties does not by itself transfer ownership; the additional “reasonably expected” requirement must also be satisfied. [CITE:1] If that requirement is not met, the invention falls under the rule that any other employee invention belongs to the employee, as between the employee and employer. [CITE:1]

These employee-invention rules apply only if, when you made the invention, you were mainly employed in Singapore, or you were not mainly employed anywhere or your place of employment could not be determined and your employer had a place of business in Singapore to which you were attached. [CITE:4] The statutory rules do not preclude an agreement or contract concerning the right to the invention from affecting ownership. [CITE:4]

In light of my finding that an express oral contract existed between the parties, the next question is whether under this contract, Mr Chin had been engaged as an employee or as a freelancer. [Employment relationships] Whether a person is an employee (as opposed to a freelancer) depends on the totality of the factual matrix of any given case. In contractual terms, the issue is whether a person is engaged under a contract of service (in which case a person would be considered an employee) or only a contract for service (in which case that person would be considered an independent contractor). There is no single test or factor which is decisive of the issue ( Kureoka Enterprise Pte Ltd v Central Provident Fund Board [1992] SGHC 113 (" Kureoka ")). In Kureoka , Chan Sek Keong J (as he then was) found the following factors relevant in the case before him: (a) the factor of control over the worker's services; (b) the rendering of services personally without being able to use a substitute; (c) the worker's responsibility for investment in, or management of, the business or financial risk in it; (d) the worker's right to price the value of services to clients; (e) the worker's opportunity to deploy individual skill and personality; (f) the contractual right to terminate the worker's services; (g) whether the worker is performing services as a person of business on his/her own account; and (h) the mutuality of obligation between the parties.

Oxel cited the English case Sabaf SpA v MFI Furniture Centres Ltd [2003] RPC 14 (" Sabaf ") on the effect of a sales contract entered into on " ex-work s " terms. In that case, an issue arose as to whether the defendant seller was liable for patent infringement on the basis that it had imported the goods into the United Kingdom. The goods in question were made in Italy and sold on " ex- works " terms to the English buyer. The English Court of Appeal held at [61] that title and risk in the goods passed as soon as the goods left the factory gate. Even though the defendant had made the relevant contract of carriage, it did so without having an ultimate interest in the goods. If property and risk had passed to the buyer before or at the beginning of the carriage, the contract of carriage is made on behalf of the buyer even if it is the seller who agrees that he will make the contract. In the present case, I accept that the contract was entered into on an " ex -works " basis and that it was Sandipala who requested Oxel to assist in arranging carriage to Jakarta for Sandipala. On this basis, based on Sab af , I am satisfied that property passed to Sandipala when each shipment of chips left Oxel's premises into the hands of the carrier or forwarder. Foot Note 321 × Ika Kusuma's Affidavit of Evidence in Chief, [46]; Closing Submissions of Oxel, [247]. On this basis, I find that the property in the chips delivered in the tenth to 15th shipments had passed to Sandipala. Accordingly, Oxel is entitled to maintain an action for the price of these chips.

question: Under the Trade Marks Act 1998, for how long is a trade mark registered?
answer: For 10 years from the date of registration, and the registration may be renewed for further periods of 10 years.

question: Can I register a brand that consists only of words describing the product's quality and kind, such as "Premium Fresh Rice"?
answer: No. Marks that consist exclusively of signs designating the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value or other characteristics of the goods must not be registered.

question: Under the Registered Designs Act 2000, how long is the initial period of registration of a design, and can it be extended?
answer: The initial period is 5 years from registration, and it may be extended for a second and a third period of 5 years each.

generated_answer:
**As at 2026-11-06, under the Registered Designs Act 2000 (Singapore), the initial period of registration of a design is 5 years, and it can be extended twice for a further 5 years each.**

### Initial period
Section 21(1) provides that the initial period of registration of a design is 5 years from the date of registration of the design [CITE:1]. A design is registered as of the date on which the application for registration was filed, and that date is deemed for the purposes of the Act to be the date of its registration [CITE:8].

### Extension
Section 21(2) provides that the period of registration may be extended for a second and third period of 5 years each [CITE:1]. If both extensions are obtained, the design can remain registered for up to 15 years from the date of registration [CITE:1].

The extension requires an application to the Registrar together with payment of the prescribed extension fee, made not earlier than the prescribed period before the expiry of the current period and not later than the date of expiry of the current period [CITE:1]. The source provided does not state how long that prescribed period is or the fee amounts, which are set by subsidiary legislation [CITE:1]. The Minister may also make rules for the Registrar to notify the registered owner before expiry of the imminent expiry and how the registration may be extended [CITE:1].

### If the extension deadline is missed
If the application and payment are not made before expiry, the registration ceases to be in force on expiry of the current period and the design must be removed from the Register [CITE:1]. However, where an extension application is made during the prescribed period after expiry and the extension fee and any prescribed late fee are paid, the registration is treated as if it had never ceased to be in force; anything done under or in relation to rights in the design during that period is treated as valid, an act that would have been an infringement is treated as an infringement, and use of the design for the services of the Government is treated as such use [CITE:1]. The Minister may also make rules for restoration of a registration that has been removed from the Register, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed [CITE:1].

### Exceptions to the general rules
- **Artistic works:** Where a registered design was, at the time of registration, a corresponding design in relation to an artistic work in which copyright subsists under the Copyright Act 2021, and by reason of previous use of that work it would not have been registrable but for section 9(1), its registration expires when the copyright in that work expires if that is earlier than it would otherwise expire, and it may not thereafter be extended [CITE:2].
- **Subsequent registrations:** A design registered under section 10(1) — for example, a later registration of an existing design in respect of other articles or non-physical products, or with modifications or variations that do not alter the character or substantially affect the identity of the design — cannot extend beyond the end of the period, and any extended period, for which the right subsists in the original design [CITE:4].

A design registered under the UK Act before 13 November 2000 is deemed to be a registered design under the Act for the article for which it was registered if the registration had not expired or been cancelled on that date [CITE:5]. The initial period for such a "relevant design" follows the transitional rules in section 77 and its Schedule, and section 21 applies, with the necessary modifications, to any further extension of the period of registration [CITE:3].

(3) Until an application has been made for registration of the prescribed particulars of a registrable transaction, the transaction is ineffective as against a person acquiring a conflicting interest in the registered design in ignorance of it. 23.—(1) After a design is registered, any person having or claiming an interest in the design may apply to the Court to determine — (a) who is the true owner of the design; (b) whether the design should have been registered in the name of the person in whose name it was registered; or (c) whether any right in the design should be transferred or granted to any other person, and the Court is to determine the question and may make such order as it considers appropriate to give effect to the determination. (2) Without limiting subsection (1), an order referred to in that subsection may contain one or more of the following directions: (a) that the name of the applicant be entered in the Register as the owner or one of the owners of the design (whether or not to the exclusion of any other person); (b) that the transaction by virtue of which that person has acquired any right in the design be registered; (c) that a licence for the use of the design be granted; (d) that the registered owner of the design or any person having any right in the design carry out such act as the Court considers appropriate to give effect to any directions in the order. (3) If any person to whom a direction referred to in subsection (2)(d) was given fails to comply with the direction within 14 days after the date of the order, the Court may, on application made to it by any person in whose favour or on whose application the order was made, authorise the second-mentioned person to do that thing on behalf of the person to whom the direction was given. (4) If an application under this section is made after the end of the period of 2 years from the date of issue of the certificate of registration referred to in section 18(c) in respect of the design in question, no order is to be made under subsection (1) transferring any right in the design from the registered owner to any other person on the ground that the registered owner was not entitled to be registered as the owner, unless it is shown that the registered owner knew at the time of the registration or of the transfer of the design to the registered owner (as the case may be) that the registered owner was not entitled to be registered as the owner. (5) The Court is not to make any order under subsection (1) unless notice of the application has first been given to — (a) the registered owner of the design; and (b) each person registered as having a right in the registered design who is not a party to the application.

question: Under the Geographical Indications Act 2014, for how long is a geographical indication registered?
answer: For 10 years from the date of registration, renewable for further periods of 10 years.

question: Under the Plant Varieties Protection Act 2004, how long does a grant of protection last?
answer: 25 calendar years from the date of the grant of protection, during which the grantee must pay an annual fee.
evidence_quote: the term of a grant of protection is a period of 25 calendar years from the date of the grant of protection
generated_answer: As at 2026-11-06, a grant of protection lasts **25 calendar years from the date of the grant**, which the Registrar must endorse on the grant, subject to the statutory provisions on invalidity and cancellation under sections 25 and 26. [CITE:1]

(2) Subject to sections 25 and 26, the term of a grant of protection is a period of 25 calendar years from the date of the grant of protection. (3) The grantee must during the term of the grant of protection pay an annual fee of a prescribed amount and furnish any information that the Registrar may require in the prescribed manner and within the prescribed period. (4) A late fee of a prescribed amount may be imposed by rules made under this Act for the payment of the annual fee within the prescribed period but after the anniversary of the date of grant of protection where the anniversary is the first day of the one year period for which the annual fee is payable, in prescribed circumstances. Scope and nature of grant of protection 28.—(1) Subject to sections 31 and 32, a grantee in respect of any protected variety is entitled to prevent a person from doing any of the following acts in respect of the propagating material of the protected variety without the authorisation, by way of a licence or otherwise, of the grantee: (a) production or reproduction; (b) conditioning for the purpose of propagation; (c) offering for sale; (d) selling or other forms of marketing; (e) export; (f) import; (g) stocking for any of the purposes specified in paragraphs (a) to (f). (2) The grantee may give an authorisation subject to conditions and limitations. (4) An assignment of a grant of protection under subsection (3) is not effective unless it is in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor. (5) Subject to subsection (6), a licence granted by a grantee in respect of any protected variety is binding on every successor in title to the grantee’s interest — (a) except any person who, in good faith and without any notice (actual or constructive) of the licence, has given valuable consideration for the interest in the grant of protection; or (b) unless the licence provides otherwise, and any reference in this Act to doing anything with, or without, the consent of the grantee is to be construed accordingly. (7) Subject to sections 31 and 32, the rights of a grantee under subsection (1) also apply to harvested material, including entire plants and parts of plants, obtained through the unauthorised use of propagating material of the protected variety unless the grantee has had a reasonable opportunity, before the harvested material was obtained, to exercise the grantee’s rights in relation to the unauthorised use of the propagating material.

question: Under the Layout-Designs of Integrated Circuits Act 1999, a layout-design created in 2010 was first commercially exploited in 2012. At the end of which year does its protection end?
answer: Because it was first exploited within 5 calendar years of creation, protection ends at the end of the 10th calendar year after 2012, that is, at the end of 2022.

“layout-design” means the 3-dimensional disposition, however expressed, of the elements of an integrated circuit (at least one of which is an active element), and of some or all of the interconnections of an integrated circuit, or such a 3-dimensional disposition prepared for an integrated circuit intended for manufacture; sources.citation: Layout-Designs of Integrated Circuits Act 1999, s 11
sources.text: 11.—(1) The rights of a qualified owner in a protected layout-design are not infringed by a person who commercially exploits, or authorises the commercial exploitation of — (a) a copy of the protected layout-design; (b) an unauthorised integrated circuit, being an integrated circuit in which the protected layout-design is incorporated; or (c) an article that contains such an integrated circuit, if, at the time when the person acquired the copy, integrated circuit or article, the person did not know, and could not be reasonably expected to have known, that the copy was unauthorised, the integrated circuit was unauthorised or that the article contained an unauthorised integrated circuit, as the case may be. (2) Where a person referred to in subsection (1) becomes aware or could reasonably be expected to become aware that the copy was unauthorised, the integrated circuit was unauthorised or that the article contains an unauthorised integrated circuit (as the case may be) that subsection continues to apply to any subsequent commercial exploitation of the copy, integrated circuit or article if and only if the person pays to the qualified owner such remuneration — (a) as is agreed; (b) as is determined by a method agreed between the person and the qualified owner; or (c) in default of agreement, as is determined by the Court on an application made by either of them. (3) In this section — (a) a copy of a protected layout-design is unauthorised if it is made without the consent of the qualified owner of the layout-design; and (b) an integrated circuit which incorporates a protected layout-design is unauthorised if such incorporation is done without the consent of the qualified owner of the layout-design.

sources.citation: Layout-Designs of Integrated Circuits Act 1999, s 6
sources.text: 6.—(1) Subject to any agreement to the contrary, the owner of a layout-design is determined as follows: (a) where the layout-design is not created pursuant to a commission or in the course of employment — the creator of a layout-design is the owner; (b) where the layout-design is created pursuant to a commission — the person who commissioned the layout-design is the owner; and (c) where the layout-design is not created pursuant to a commission but is created by an employee in the course of his or her employment — the employer is the owner. (2) A qualified person can be a qualified owner even if the qualified person shares ownership with a person who is not a qualified person. (3) Where a layout-design is owned by more than one person, references in the Act to the owner are to all the owners and references in the Act to the qualified owner are to all the qualified owners so that in particular, any requirement of the consent of a qualified owner requires the consent of all the qualified owners.

sources.citation: Layout-Designs of Integrated Circuits Act 1999, s 28
sources.text: 28.—(1) A licence granted under section 27 is — (a) both non-exclusive and non-assignable; (b) subject to the payment to the qualified owner of the remuneration specified in the Court order under section 27(3). (2) An act done pursuant to a licence granted under section 27 in relation to a protected layout-design is not to be taken into account in calculating the duration of protection of the layout-design under section 7.

sources.citation: Layout-Designs of Integrated Circuits Act 1999, s 24
sources.text: 24.—(1) The right to do an act in relation to a protected layout-design under section 23 — (a) is both non-exclusive and non-assignable; (b) is limited to a public non-commercial purpose; (c) is subject to the terms of any authorisation under that section; (d) does not permit the sale of the layout-design, a copy of the layout-design, or an integrated circuit in which the layout-design is incorporated (whether or not the integrated circuit is contained in another article) to the public; and (e) is limited to the doing of the act predominantly in Singapore. (2) An act done under section 23 in relation to a protected layout-design is not to be taken into account in calculating the duration of protection of the layout-design under section 7.

In any proceedings to enforce a qualified owner’s rights under this Part, it is presumed, unless a defendant puts the matter in issue, that in respect of the layout-design that is the subject matter of the proceedings — (a) the claimant is a qualified owner of the layout-design; and [Act 25 of 2021 wef 01/04/2022] (b) the layout-design is a protected layout-design.

sources.citation: Layout-Designs of Integrated Circuits Act 1999, s 10
sources.text: 10. It is not an infringement of a qualified owner’s right in a protected layout-design — (a) if the copying is of any part of a protected layout-design that does not comply with the requirement of originality referred to in section 5(1); (b) if the copying is done for a private purpose and not for the purpose of commercial exploitation; (c) if the copying is done for the sole purpose of evaluation, analysis, research or teaching; (d) to use the results of such evaluation, analysis or research to create a different layout-design that complies with the requirement of originality referred to in section 5(1); (e) to do any of the acts referred to in section 8 in respect of the layout-design referred to in paragraph (d); (f) for a qualified owner of another protected layout-design — (i) that is identical to the firstmentioned protected layout-design; and (ii) that is independently created, to do any of the acts referred to in section 8 in respect of that other layout-design; or (g) to commercially exploit a copy of the protected layout-design, an integrated circuit in which the layout-design is incorporated or an article that contains an integrated circuit in which the layout-design is incorporated after the copy, integrated circuit or article has been commercially exploited, whether in Singapore or elsewhere, by, or with the consent of, the qualified owner.

sources.citation: Layout-Designs of Integrated Circuits Act 1999, s 20
sources.text: 20.—(1) An exclusive licensee has the same rights against a successor in title to the qualified owner as the exclusive licensee has against the grantor of the licence. (2) An exclusive licensee has, except against the qualified owner, the same rights and remedies in respect of matters occurring after the grant of the exclusive licence as if the licence had been an assignment. (3) An exclusive licensee’s rights and remedies are concurrent with those of the qualified owner. (4) In any proceedings brought by an exclusive licensee, a defendant may avail himself, herself or itself of any defence that would have been available to the defendant if the proceedings had been brought by the qualified owner.

sources.citation: Layout-Designs of Integrated Circuits Act 1999, s 13
sources.text: 13.—(1) Where a person has in the person’s possession, custody or control — (a) for commercial exploitation purposes an integrated circuit in which a protected layout-design is incorporated; or (b) any article which the person knows or has reason to believe has been or is to be predominantly used to make integrated circuits in which a protected layout-design is incorporated, a qualified owner of the protected layout-design may apply to the Court for an order that the integrated circuit or article referred to in paragraph (b) be delivered to the qualified owner or to another person that the Court specifies. (2) The Court may not make an order for delivery up unless it also makes, or it appears to the Court that there are grounds for making, an order under section 14. (3) A person to whom an integrated circuit or an article referred to in subsection (1)(b) is delivered up must, if an order under section 14 is not made at the time of the order under this section, retain the integrated circuit or article pending the making of an order, or a decision not to make an order, under section 14.

sources.text: 1. This Act is the Layout-Designs of Integrated Circuits Act 1999.

sources.citation: Layout-Designs of Integrated Circuits Act 1999, s 18
sources.text: 18.—(1) A right in a layout-design is movable property and is transmissible by any means by which such property may be lawfully transmitted including assignment, licence, testamentary instrument and operation of law. (2) An assignment or transmission may be total or partial. (3) An assignment is ineffective unless it is in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor. (4) A licence granted in respect of a layout-design right by a qualified owner binds each successor in title to the qualified owner’s interest in the right, except a purchaser in good faith for value without notice (actual or constructive) of the licence and a person who derives title from the purchaser.

sources.citation: Layout-Designs of Integrated Circuits Act 1999, s 19
sources.text: 19.—(1) Where, by an agreement made in relation to a future right in a layout-design that is signed by or on behalf of the person who would be the owner of the right on its coming into existence, the person purports to assign the future right in the layout-design, wholly or partially, to an assignee, the right, on coming into existence, vests in the assignee or the assignee’s successor in title. (2) Where, at the time when a layout-design right comes into existence, the person who would be entitled to the right is dead, the right devolves as if, immediately before the person’s death, the person had been the owner of the right. (3) A licence granted in respect of a future layout-design right by a prospective qualified owner binds each successor in title to his or her interest (or prospective interest) in the right, except a purchaser in good faith for value without notice (actual or constructive) of the licence and a person who derives title from the purchaser.

sources.text: 39E.—(1) Where section 39C applies, any tax chargeable at the new rate on the separate supply must be accounted for in the prescribed accounting period in which the earliest of the following falls: (a) the date of any new invoice for the amount on which the tax at the new rate is charged; (b) the date any consideration is received towards the amount on which the tax at the new rate is charged; (c) the last day of the period of 14 days or any longer period that the Comptroller may allow, after the date of the specified change. (2) Despite subsection (1), where a recipient applies section 11C(3) to its reverse charge supplies, the recipient must account for any tax chargeable at the new rate (less any tax on the supply already accounted for) on each reverse charge supply in the prescribed accounting period in which the earlier of the following falls for that supply: (a) the date any consideration is paid by the recipient towards the amount on which the tax at the new rate is chargeable; (b) the last day of the period of 14 days or any longer period that the Comptroller may allow, after the date of the specified change. (3) Despite subsection (1), where a recipient makes an election under section 11C(8) in relation to its reverse charge supplies, the recipient must account for any tax chargeable at the new rate (less any tax on the supply already accounted for) on each reverse charge supply in the prescribed accounting period in which the following falls for that supply: (a) if the day immediately after the end of the longer period is on or after the date of the specified change — that day; (b) if the day immediately after the end of the longer period is before the date of the specified change — the last day of the period of 14 days or any longer period that the Comptroller may allow, after the date of the specified change. sources.text: 21.—(1) Subject to this section and sections 21A, 21B and 21C, a supply of goods is zero‑rated only if the goods are exported and a supply of services is zero‑rated only if the services are international services. [28/2007; 19/2012] (2) Where a taxable person supplies goods or services and the supply is zero‑rated, then, whether or not tax would be chargeable on the supply apart from this section — (a) no tax is charged on the supply; but (b) it is in all other respects treated as a taxable supply, and accordingly the rate at which tax is treated as charged on the supply is nil. (3) A supply of services is treated as a supply of international services where the services or the supply are for the time being of any of the following descriptions: (a) services (not being ancillary transport activities such as loading, unloading and handling) comprising the transport of passengers or goods — (i) in the case of transport by air or land, where the transportation is — (A) from a place outside Singapore to another place outside Singapore; (B) from a place in Singapore to a place outside Singapore; or (C) from a place outside Singapore to a place in Singapore; and (ii) in the case of transport by sea, where the transportation is — (A) from a place outside Singapore to another place outside Singapore; or (B) from a place in Singapore or to a place in Singapore, and substantially outside Singapore; (iii) [Deleted by Act 20 of 2010] (b) services (including any ancillary transport activities such as loading, unloading and handling) comprising the transport of goods from a place in Singapore to another place in Singapore to the extent that those services are supplied by the same supplier as part of the supply of services to which paragraph (a)(i) and (ii) (other than in relation to any transportation that is from a place outside Singapore to another place outside Singapore) applies; (c) services (other than the letting on hire of any means of transport) — (i) supplied before 1 January 2023, and comprising the insuring or the arranging of the insurance or the arranging of the transport of passengers or goods to which any provision of paragraphs (a) and (b) applies; or (ii) supplied on or after 1 January 2023, and comprising — (A) the insuring of the transport of passengers to whom any provision of paragraph (a) applies; or (B) the insuring or the arranging of the insurance or the arranging of the transport of goods, to which any provision of paragraphs (a) and (b) applies

sources.text: 93.—(1) Where an invoice for a supply in fact made that gives rise to a reverse charge supply was or is issued on or after 19 February 2018 but before 1 January 2020, tax is chargeable on the reverse charge supply to the extent of — (a) the amount of the invoice paid on or after 1 January 2020; or (b) the value of the services to which the invoice relates that are performed on or after 1 January 2020, if lower. [33/2019] (5) Subsection (4) does not apply if the whole amount of the invoice is paid, and the whole of the services is performed, on or after 1 January 2020. [33/2019] (6) For the purposes of this section, where only a part of the services in fact supplied is performed, the value of the part is a value that is, in the opinion of the Comptroller, reasonably attributable to the part. [33/2019] (7) Where the reverse charge supply in subsection (1) or (4) spans one or more other specified changes within the meaning of section 39(3), then tax is chargeable on the chargeable value of the reverse charge supply in accordance with Division 1 of Part 6A. question: Under the Payroll Tax Act 1965, how is an amount of payroll tax that contains a fraction of a dollar treated?
answer: The tax payable is taken to be that amount less the fraction of a dollar.
evidence_quote: the tax payable shall be taken to be that amount less that fraction
generated_answer: As at 2026-11-06, any fraction of a dollar contained in the payroll tax amount is removed. For example, if the tax calculated is $100.50, the amount payable is $100. [CITE:1]

(2) The secretary, manager, principal officer or any director in Singapore of every company and the secretary, manager, principal officer or other officer in Singapore of every body of persons shall be answerable for doing all such acts, matters and things relating to payroll tax as are required to be done by this Act or any regulations made thereunder by that company or body of persons. (3) The Comptroller may by notice in writing, if he thinks it necessary, declare any person to be the agent of any employer and the person so declared to be the agent shall be the agent of the employer for the purpose of this Act, and may be required to pay any payroll tax due from any moneys which may be held by him for, or due by him to, the employer whose agent he has been declared to be. (4) Every person answerable under this Act for the payment of payroll tax on behalf of an employer may retain out of any money coming to his hands on behalf of the employer so much thereof as shall be sufficient to pay the tax; and he shall be and is hereby indemnified against any person whatsoever for all payments made by him under this Act or any regulations made thereunder.

question: Under the Property Tax Act 1960, what is the standard rate of property tax?
answer: 36% of the annual value of every property in the Valuation List, although the Minister may set lower rates for prescribed properties.

question: The Chief Assessor sent me a notice asking for a return with details about my property. How long do I have to submit it?
answer: The return must be made within 21 days from the date of the notice; failing to comply is an offence.
evidence_quote: a notice requiring the person to make within 21 days from the date of the notice a return
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, if the Chief Assessor has served a notice under section 16(1) of the Property Tax Act 1960 requiring a return, you must submit the return **within 21 days from the date of the notice**. [CITE:1]

The return must use the form prescribed by the Chief Assessor and contain the required particulars. [CITE:1] Failure to comply with the notice is an offence punishable on conviction by a fine not exceeding $1,000. [CITE:1]

For this purpose:

- A message is “unsolicited” if the recipient did not request it or consent to receiving it; merely providing or publishing the recipient’s electronic address does not amount to a request or consent. [CITE:7]

This Act is to be construed consistently with what is commercially reasonable under the circumstances and to give effect to the following purposes: (a) to facilitate electronic communications by means of reliable electronic records; (b) to facilitate electronic commerce, to eliminate barriers to electronic commerce resulting from uncertainties over writing and signature requirements, and to promote the development of the legal and business infrastructure necessary to implement secure electronic commerce; (c) to facilitate electronic filing of documents with public agencies, and to promote efficient delivery by public agencies of services by means of reliable electronic records; (d) to minimise the incidence of forged electronic records, intentional and unintentional alteration of records, and fraud in electronic commerce and other electronic transactions; (e) to help to establish uniformity of rules, regulations and standards regarding the authentication and integrity of electronic records; (f) to promote public confidence in the integrity and reliability of electronic records and electronic commerce, and to foster the development of electronic commerce through the use of electronic signatures to lend authenticity and integrity to correspondence in any electronic medium; (g) to implement the United Nations Convention on the Use of Electronic Communications in International Contracts adopted by the General Assembly of the United Nations on 23 November 2005 and to make the law of Singapore on electronic transactions, whether or not involving parties whose places of business are in different States, consistent with the provisions of that Convention; (h) to adopt the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Transferable Records adopted by the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law on 13 July 2017 in its application to an electronic transferable record, whether the electronic transferable record is issued or used in Singapore or outside Singapore. question: My company has assessed that a data breach is serious enough that it must be reported to the regulator. How soon must we report it?
answer: The organisation must notify the Commission as soon as practicable, and no later than 3 calendar days after the day it made that assessment.
evidence_quote: no later than 3 calendar days after the day the organisation makes that assessment
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, if your company has assessed the breach under section 26C and determined that it is a **notifiable data breach**, it must notify the Commission **as soon as practicable, and no later than 3 calendar days after the day the assessment was made**. [CITE:1][CITE:2]

A breach is notifiable if it results or is likely to result in significant harm to an affected individual, or is or is likely to be of significant scale. [CITE:4] The three-day period is an outer limit; notification may still be required sooner under the “as soon as is practicable” standard. [CITE:1]

If your company is a data intermediary processing personal data for another organisation, it must notify that organisation **without undue delay**, after which the organisation notified must assess whether the breach is notifiable. [CITE:2]

HLT argued that it had a viable case on the Reporting Duty Claim. Similar to the Creditor Duty, HLT submitted that it was incorrect to limit the scope of Deloitte's duty to the reporting of accurate information to HLT's shareholders (see [20] above). In some cases, an auditor's duty would extend to reporting any fraud or irregularity that was likely to result in material loss to the company to either the directors of the company or to a third party directly, especially where the auditor suspected that the management of the company was involved in the fraud or irregularity. The existence of the Reporting Duty was also supported by the relevant statutory framework which contained provisions that imposed on auditors an obligation in certain circumstances to report fraud or irregularities in the company's affairs to persons outside of the company. These included: (a) s 207(9) of the CA; and (b) s 39(1) of the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act (Cap 65A, 2000 Rev Ed) (which made it mandatory for a person to lodge a suspicious transaction report if information or matters came to his attention in the course of his trade, profession, business or employment gave him reason to suspect that certain property was linked to criminal conduct). Moreover, the content of the Reporting Duty was not limited to matters within Deloitte's actual knowledge but also included matters which would have come to its knowledge had it acted with reasonable skill and competence. This is because, HLT argued, the Reporting Duty was "founded on a claim for breach of [a] duty of care". We pause here to make the observation again that, seeing as HLT's own submission located the Reporting Duty within Deloitte's "duty of care", it is far from clear how the Reporting Duty Claim is distinct from the Negligence Claim and why the parties have continued to proceed on this basis.

question: Under the Personal Data Protection Act 2012, when may an organisation collect, use or disclose personal data about an individual?
answer: Only if the individual gives or is deemed to have given consent, or if doing so without consent is required or authorised under the Act or another written law.
evidence_quote: the individual gives, or is deemed to have given, his or her consent under this Act to the collection, use or disclosure
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, based on the supplied consolidated version stated to be in force from 2025-12-05, an organisation may generally collect, use or disclose an individual’s personal data only if the individual has consented or is deemed to have consented, unless the processing without consent is required or authorised by the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 or another written law. [CITE:3]

### 1. Consent-based processing

For actual consent, the individual must first be given the information required by section 20 and then consent to the particular collection, use or disclosure. [CITE:12]

An organisation cannot make consent to processing beyond what is reasonably necessary to provide a product or service a condition of supplying that product or service. [CITE:12]

Consent obtained through false or misleading information, deceptive practices, or misleading practices generally is not validly given. [CITE:12]

Consent may also be deemed to exist in two circumstances:

- Under section 15, consent is deemed where an individual voluntarily provides personal data for a purpose and it is reasonable that the individual would voluntarily provide the data for that purpose. [CITE:17]
- Under section 15A, deemed consent by notification applies where the organisation assesses that the proposed processing is not likely to have an adverse effect on the individual, takes reasonable steps to inform the individual of the intended processing and its purpose, gives the individual a reasonable period and manner to object, and the individual does not object within that period. [CITE:7]

### 2. Processing without consent

Section 17 permits collection, use or disclosure without consent in the circumstances specified in the First Schedule or the relevant Part of the Second Schedule, subject to the stated conditions. [CITE:2]

The schedules distinguish between:

- Collection without consent, under the First Schedule or Part 1 of the Second Schedule. [CITE:2]
- Use without consent, under the First Schedule or Part 2 of the Second Schedule. [CITE:2]
- Disclosure without consent, under the First Schedule or Part 3 of the Second Schedule. [CITE:2]

Examples expressly shown in the supplied provisions include:

- Processing necessary for a purpose clearly in the individual’s interests where consent cannot be obtained in time or the individual would not reasonably be expected to withhold consent. [CITE:15]
- Processing necessary to respond to an emergency threatening life, health or safety, and certain processing where consent cannot be obtained in time and there are reasonable grounds to believe serious harm to health or safety will result. [CITE:5]
- Processing of publicly available personal data, processing in the national interest, and news-organisation processing solely for its news activity, subject to the applicable conditions. [CITE:5]
- Processing in the organisation’s or another person’s legitimate interests where those interests outweigh any adverse effect on the individual, supported by a prior assessment and reasonable measures to eliminate, reduce or mitigate that effect. [CITE:4]
- Processing reasonably connected with entering into, managing or terminating an employment relationship or appointment. [CITE:6]
- Processing connected with a business asset transaction, subject to the transaction-specific conditions in the First Schedule. [CITE:6][CITE:13]
- Collection or use of personal data disclosed by a public agency where the processing is consistent with the purpose of that disclosure. [CITE:9]
- Business-improvement use, including service or process improvement, behavioural understanding, and personalisation, where the purpose cannot reasonably be achieved without individually identifiable data and a reasonable person would consider the use appropriate. [CITE:9]
- Research use or disclosure satisfying the statutory conditions, including identifiable data being necessary, a clear public benefit, research results not affecting the individual, and non-identifying published results. [CITE:14]

Where an organisation collects personal data from another organisation without the individual’s consent, it must give the other organisation sufficient information about the collection purpose to allow that organisation to determine whether the disclosure complies with the Act. [CITE:10]

### 3. Appropriate purpose and notification

Whether processing is based on consent or a statutory exception, it must be for a purpose that a reasonable person would consider appropriate in the circumstances. [CITE:1]

Where section 20 applies, the organisation must inform the individual of the collection, use or disclosure purposes on or before collection, and inform the individual of any new use or disclosure purpose before that processing occurs. [CITE:10]

The organisation must also provide the business contact information of an appropriate representative if the individual requests it. [CITE:10]

The ordinary section 20 notification requirement does not apply to deemed consent under sections 15 or 15A, or to processing without consent under section 17. [CITE:10]

Section 15A nevertheless requires its own advance assessment and notification steps, while employment-related collection, use or disclosure remains subject to a separate notification requirement. [CITE:7][CITE:10]

### 4. Withdrawal of consent

An individual may withdraw consent at any time by giving reasonable notice. [CITE:16]

After receiving the notice, the organisation must inform the individual of the likely consequences of withdrawal and must cease the affected collection, use or disclosure unless that processing without consent is independently required or authorised by the Act or another written law. [CITE:16]

### Scope

The statutory provisions containing these rules do not impose the same obligations on individuals acting personally or domestically, employees acting in the course of employment, or public agencies, and business contact information is generally outside their scope unless expressly mentioned. [CITE:19]

In short, processing must rest on valid consent, deemed consent, or an applicable statutory or other-law exception, and must remain within the reasonable-purpose and applicable notification and withdrawal rules. [CITE:3][CITE:1][CITE:10][CITE:16]

question: How long can a company keep my personal details after it no longer needs them?
answer: It must stop retaining them, or remove the means of linking them to individuals, as soon as it is reasonable to assume the purpose is no longer served and retention is not needed for legal or business purposes.
evidence_quote: retention is no longer necessary for legal or business purposes
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, Singapore’s Personal Data Protection Act does not prescribe one fixed period in years or months for retaining personal data after its original purpose has ended. [CITE:1]

A company must stop retaining documents containing personal data—or remove the means of associating the data with identifiable individuals—once it is reasonable to assume that both of the following are true: the purpose for collecting the data is no longer served by retaining it, and retention is no longer necessary for legal or business purposes. [CITE:1]

Consequently, the company cannot justify continued retention merely by saying that records might be useful in future; continued retention must still be reasonably necessary for a legal or business purpose. [CITE:1]

While the personal data is retained, the company must make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, use, disclosure, alteration or disposal, and to prevent loss of the storage medium or device containing it. [CITE:2]

There is one specific exception concerning an individual’s access request: if an individual makes an access request on or after 1 February 2021 and the company refuses to provide the personal data, the company must preserve a complete and accurate copy for at least the prescribed period. The supplied provisions do not state the length of that prescribed period; it must be checked in the applicable regulations on Singapore Statutes Online or with a lawyer. [CITE:3]

question: Under the Personal Data Protection Act 2012, how must an organisation protect personal data in its possession or control?
answer: By making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal, and the loss of any storage medium or device holding the data.

question: Before a business sends a marketing message to my Singapore phone number, what must it check?
answer: It must have valid confirmation, at the time of sending, that the Singapore telephone number is not listed in the relevant register.

question: Under the Competition Act 2004, which agreements between undertakings are prohibited?
answer: Agreements, decisions or concerted practices whose object or effect is to prevent, restrict or distort competition within Singapore, unless they are exempt.

As at 2026-11-06, under the supplied consolidated text, section 34(1) of the Competition Act 2004 prohibits an agreement between undertakings if it has as its object or effect the prevention, restriction or distortion of competition within Singapore, unless it is exempt in accordance with Part 3 of the Act. [CITE:1]

### Prohibited agreements

Section 34(2) gives non-exhaustive examples of agreements that may have that prohibited object or effect, including agreements that: [CITE:1]

- directly or indirectly fix purchase or selling prices or other trading conditions; [CITE:1]
- limit or control production, markets, technical development or investment; [CITE:1]
- share markets or sources of supply; [CITE:1]
- apply dissimilar conditions to equivalent transactions with other trading parties, placing those parties at a competitive disadvantage; or [CITE:1]
- make the conclusion of contracts subject to acceptance of supplementary obligations that, by their nature or commercial usage, have no connection with the subject of those contracts. [CITE:1]

The same prohibition also applies to decisions by associations of undertakings and concerted practices. [CITE:1] Any provision of a prohibited agreement is void to the extent that it infringes section 34(1). [CITE:1]

### Exclusions and exemptions

Section 35 provides that the section 34 prohibition does not apply to matters specified in the Third Schedule. [CITE:3] The Third Schedule includes exclusions for: [CITE:4] [CITE:10]

- an agreement made to comply with a legal requirement, meaning a requirement imposed by or under any written law; [CITE:4]
- a particular agreement, or category of agreement, excluded by ministerial order to avoid a conflict with Singapore’s international obligations; [CITE:4]
- an undertaking entrusted with operating services of general economic interest, or having the character of a revenue-producing monopoly, insofar as the prohibition would obstruct the performance of its assigned tasks; [CITE:4]
- an agreement relating to specified activities, including licensed postal services, piped potable water, wastewater management, licensed bus and rail services, and licensed cargo-terminal operations; [CITE:10]
- an agreement relating to goods or services to the extent that another written law, or a code of practice issued under written law, gives another regulatory authority jurisdiction over the matter; [CITE:10]
- a vertical agreement, meaning an agreement between undertakings operating at different levels of the production or distribution chain concerning purchase, sale or resale conditions, unless the Minister specifies that agreement by order. [CITE:10]

A separate block-exemption mechanism can exempt a category of agreements. [CITE:9] If, in the Commission’s opinion, agreements in a category are likely to satisfy section 41, the Commission may recommend that the Minister make an order specifying that category, and the Minister may make the order in the recommended form or with modifications. [CITE:9] The section 41 criteria are that the agreement contributes to improving production or distribution, or promotes technical or economic progress, without imposing restrictions that are not indispensable to those objectives or allowing the undertakings concerned the possibility of eliminating competition for a substantial part of the goods or services concerned. [CITE:2]

### Territorial reach

Part 3 applies even where an agreement was entered into outside Singapore or a party is outside Singapore, if the agreement infringes or has infringed the section 34 prohibition. [CITE:8] Part 3 also does not apply to an agreement entered into by the Government, a statutory body, or a person acting on their behalf in relation to that agreement. [CITE:8]

Section 54(1) of the Competition Act 2004 prohibits mergers that have resulted or may be expected to result in a “substantial lessening of competition” within any market in Singapore for goods or services, subject to the statutory exclusions. Company size alone is not the stated legal test. [CITE:1]

A transaction may constitute a merger if previously independent undertakings merge, control over an undertaking is acquired, or an asset acquisition places the buyer in a position to replace the acquired business; a lasting joint venture performing all the functions of an autonomous economic entity may also qualify. [CITE:1]

The prohibition does not apply in specified circumstances, including:

- approval by a Minister or regulatory authority, or the exercise of jurisdiction by another regulatory authority, under written law; [CITE:2]
- a merger involving an undertaking relating to a specified activity under the Third Schedule; and [CITE:2]
- a merger for which the economic efficiencies arising or expected to arise outweigh its adverse effects on competition in the relevant Singapore market. [CITE:2]

A party may notify the Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore and apply for a decision concerning an anticipated merger or a merger already carried out. The Commission then decides whether the section 54 prohibition will be, or has been, infringed. [CITE:11][CITE:5] If the Commission proposes to find infringement, the relevant party may, within 14 days, apply to the Minister for a public-interest exemption, and the Minister’s decision is final. [CITE:11][CITE:5]

The Commission may also accept commitments to take or refrain from taking action to remedy, mitigate or prevent the substantial lessening of competition or its adverse effects; an accepted commitment can lead to a decision that the prohibition has not been infringed, subject to the statutory grounds for revocation. [CITE:6][CITE:16]

If the Commission finds that the prohibition has been infringed, it may prohibit an anticipated merger from being carried into effect or require a completed merger to be dissolved or modified as it directs. [CITE:4] The Act may also apply where the merger occurs outside Singapore if it infringes, or would if carried out infringe, the section 54 prohibition. [CITE:10]

[23/2007] (2) For the purposes of this Part, a merger occurs if — (a) 2 or more undertakings, previously independent of one another, merge; (b) one or more persons or other undertakings acquire direct or indirect control of the whole or part of one or more other undertakings; or (c) the result of an acquisition by one undertaking (the first undertaking) of the assets (including goodwill), or a substantial part of the assets, of another undertaking (the second undertaking) is to place the first undertaking in a position to replace or substantially replace the second undertaking in the business or, as appropriate, the part concerned of the business in which that undertaking was engaged immediately before the acquisition. [23/2007] (3) For the purposes of this Part, control is, in relation to an undertaking, regarded as existing if, by reason of rights, contracts or any other means, or any combination of rights, contracts or other means, decisive influence is capable of being exercised with regard to the activities of the undertaking and, in particular, by — (a) ownership of, or the right to use all or part of, the assets of an undertaking; or (b) rights or contracts which enable decisive influence to be exercised with regard to the composition, voting or decisions of the organs of an undertaking. [23/2007] (4) For the purposes of this Part, control is acquired by any person or other undertaking if that person or undertaking — (a) becomes a holder of the rights or contracts, or entitled to use the other means, referred to in subsection (3); or (b) although not becoming such a holder or entitled to use those other means, acquires the power to exercise the rights derived therefrom. [23/2007] (5) The creation of a joint venture to perform, on a lasting basis, all the functions of an autonomous economic entity constitutes a merger falling within subsection (2)(b). [23/2007] (6) In determining whether influence of the kind referred to in subsection (3) is capable of being exercised, regard must be had to all the circumstances of the matter and not solely to the legal effect of any instrument, deed, transfer, assignment or other act done or made. question: Under the Casino Control Act 2006, how long does a casino licence remain in force?
answer: For the period for which it is granted, as specified in the licence, unless it is cancelled or surrendered sooner.
evidence_quote: A casino licence remains in force for the period for which it is granted, as specified in the licence
generated_answer:
**As at 2026-11-06, under the Casino Control Act 2006, a casino licence remains in force for the period for which it is granted, as specified in the licence itself, unless it is sooner cancelled or surrendered under the Act [CITE:1].** The duration is therefore determined by the term stated in the particular licence, rather than by one fixed period stated in these provisions [CITE:1] [CITE:4].

### How the term is fixed
When the Authority grants an application, the licence is granted for the term, subject to the conditions and for the location specified in the licence [CITE:4]. Conditions may be imposed as the Authority thinks fit, provided they are not inconsistent with a provision of the Act [CITE:4]. The conditions themselves may later be amended, varied, revoked, or supplemented, following the procedure in section 50 [CITE:19].

### Ways a licence can end before its stated term
- **Surrender:** A casino operator may surrender the licence by giving written notice to the Authority, but the surrender takes effect only if the Authority consents to it [CITE:11].
- **Cancellation by the Minister:** After consulting the Authority, the Minister may cancel any casino licence where it appears necessary in the public interest, and must give directions to give effect to the cancellation [CITE:9]. Any licence or approval granted under the Act is in any event a revocable privilege [CITE:10].
- **Lapse for non-payment of the licence fee:** Despite section 52, the licence lapses if any part of the casino licence fee is not paid within the time prescribed for payment [CITE:5].

### Renewal
An application for renewal must be made to the Authority in the Authority's specified form not later than six months before the expiry date, accompanied by the prescribed renewal application fee and any documents and information the Authority requires [CITE:7]. An application submitted less than six months before expiry must additionally carry the prescribed late application fee [CITE:7]. Sections 44 to 49, which govern a new licence application, apply to a renewal application with the necessary modifications [CITE:7].

### Related points
- A person must not operate a casino without a valid casino licence in force, and contravention is an offence punishable by fine and/or imprisonment [CITE:6].
- The Act requires the Authority, up to and including 31 December 2030, to ensure that no more than two casino licences are in force at any one time, and each licence applies to one casino only [CITE:2].
- If a licence is cancelled, surrendered, or suspended, the Authority may, with the Minister's approval, appoint a manager of the casino, who is deemed the holder of the licence on the same terms as the former operator, subject to modifications the Authority determines [CITE:8].
- Disciplinary proceedings begun against a casino operator may continue, and further disciplinary action may be taken, even after the licence has been cancelled, surrendered, or expired [CITE:12].

question: Under the Trade Unions Act 1940, within what period must a newly established trade union apply for registration?
answer: Within one month from the date on which it is established, unless the Registrar extends the period.

[CITE:1] The union is established on the first date when any workmen or employers agree to create the association or combination for the relevant trade-union objects. [CITE:1]

question: Under the Industrial Relations Act 1960, can a trade union of employees serve a notice under section 18 on an employer that has not recognised it?
answer: No. A trade union of employees that has not been given recognition by the employer in the prescribed manner may not serve that employer such a notice.
evidence_quote: No trade union of employees which has not been given recognition by an employer in the prescribed manner may serve on that employer a notice under section 18
generated_answer: As at 2026-11-06, no. Section 17(1) of the Industrial Relations Act 1960 prohibits a trade union of employees that has not been given recognition by the employer in the prescribed manner from serving that employer with a notice under section 18 [CITE:2]. This is consistent with section 18, which permits a trade union to serve an invitation to negotiate only if it “has been accorded recognition by an employer” [CITE:1].

sources.text: 18.—(1) A trade union of employees which has been accorded recognition by an employer may serve on that employer or an employer may serve on a trade union of employees a notice in the prescribed form — (a) setting out proposals for a collective agreement in relation to any industrial matters; and (b) inviting the employer or trade union of employees, as the case may be, to negotiate with it in relation to those matters with a view to arriving at a collective agreement. (2) Notwithstanding subsection (1), no trade union of employees may include in a notice setting out proposals for a collective agreement a proposal in relation to any of the following matters: (a) the promotion by an employer of any employee from a lower grade or category to a higher grade or category; (b) the transfer by an employer of an employee within the organisation of an employer’s profession, business, trade or work, provided that such transfer does not entail a change to the detriment of an employee in regard to his terms of employment; (c) the employment by an employer of any person that he may appoint in the event of a vacancy arising in his establishment; (d) the termination by an employer of the services of an employee by reason of redundancy or by reason of the reorganisation of an employer’s profession, business, trade or work or the criteria for such termination; (e) the dismissal and reinstatement of an employee by an employer in circumstances in which section 35(3) applies; (f) the assignment or allocation by an employer of duties or specific tasks to an employee that are consistent or compatible with the terms of his employment.

question: During a trade dispute, is it lawful for union members to gather near a workplace just to peacefully pass on information?
answer: Yes. Attending at or near a place where a person works merely to peacefully obtain or communicate information in furtherance of a trade dispute is not unlawful, subject to limits such as attending in intimidating numbers.

As at 2026-11-06, **yes — gathering near a workplace during a trade dispute for the purpose of peacefully passing on information is generally lawful**, subject to the limits set out below. [CITE:1]

**The general rule (section 10 of the Trade Disputes Act 1941, headed "Picketing")**

- It is not unlawful for one or more persons acting on their own behalf, or on behalf of a trade union (or, in a platform-work context, a platform work association or an individual platform operator), in contemplation or furtherance of a trade dispute or work dispute, to attend at or near a house or place where a person resides, works, or carries on business, or at the approach to such a place, merely for the purpose of peacefully obtaining or communicating information. [CITE:1]
- The wording extends to attending "at or near" the workplace and to its approach, so peaceful information-sharing outside the workplace is covered by the same permission. [CITE:1]
- Section 10 was amended with effect from 1 January 2025 to extend these provisions to platform work associations, individual platform operators, and work disputes. [CITE:1] [CITE:8]
- A "trade dispute" is defined broadly as any dispute between employers and workmen, between workmen and workmen, or between employers and employers that is connected with employment or non-employment, or the terms or conditions of work, of any person. [CITE:12]

**When the gathering would be unlawful**

Attending in such numbers, or otherwise in such a manner, as to be calculated to do any of the following makes the attendance unlawful, and it is then deemed to constitute an offence under section 9(d) of the Trade Disputes Act 1941: [CITE:1]

- intimidate any person in that house or place; [CITE:1]
- obstruct the approach to or exit from that house or place; [CITE:1]
- lead to a breach of the peace. [CITE:1]

Section 15 of the Trade Disputes Act 1941 provides that an agreement or combination to do such an act is not punishable as a conspiracy if one person doing it would not be a crime, but it does not exempt any conspiracy punishable under written law and does not affect the law relating to riot, unlawful assembly, breach of the peace, or offences against the State or the President. question: Do I need a licence to run a shop that buys and resells used goods?
answer: Yes. A person must not deal in secondhand goods except under, and in accordance with, a licence; doing so without one is an offence.

question: Is it legal to join a pyramid selling scheme in Singapore?
answer: No. It is unlawful to promote or participate in a multi-level marketing or pyramid selling scheme, punishable by a fine of up to $200,000, up to 5 years' imprisonment, or both.
gold_citations: Multi-Level Marketing and Pyramid Selling (Prohibition) Act 1973, s 3
evidence_quote: It is unlawful for any person to promote or participate in a multi-level marketing scheme or arrangement or a pyramid selling scheme or arrangement
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, **no—if “join” means becoming a participant in or taking part in the scheme.** Section 3(1) makes it unlawful for any person to promote or participate in a pyramid selling scheme or arrangement, or to hold out that they are doing so. [CITE:4]

The Act treats a “multi-level marketing scheme or arrangement” as having the same meaning as a “pyramid selling scheme or arrangement”. [CITE:6]

A statutory pyramid selling scheme involves the distribution or purported distribution of a commodity where a participant may acquire the commodity, or a right or licence to acquire it, for distribution; receives a benefit from the recruitment or sales activities of additional participants; and another promoter or participant may also receive a benefit. [CITE:6]

Contravening section 3 is an offence punishable on conviction by a fine of up to **$200,000**, imprisonment for up to **five years**, or both. [CITE:4]

If “join” means only making an isolated retail purchase rather than participating in or promoting the scheme, the supplied statutory provisions do not expressly resolve that distinction. [CITE:6]

question: Under the Foreign Employee Dormitories Act 2015, what is required to operate boarding premises as a foreign employee dormitory?
answer: A valid licence for those premises, unless an exemption applies.
evidence_quote: a person must not operate any boarding premises as a foreign employee dormitory except under the authority of a valid licence for those premises
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, the core requirement is that, unless exempted under section 32, a person may operate boarding premises as a foreign employee dormitory only under the authority of a valid licence for those premises; a proprietor must not use or permit the premises as a foreign employee dormitory unless it is operated by a licensed operator holding a valid licence relating to those premises. [CITE:1]

### 1. Whether the premises come within the Act

“Boarding premises” means premises providing boarders or lodgers with a principal place of residence, which may have shared facilities or services and rooms accommodating one or more boarders or lodgers. [CITE:14]

A foreign employee dormitory is boarding premises that:

- provide at least the prescribed threshold number of beds for foreign employees; or
- accommodate at least that number of foreign-employee residents; or
- have the prescribed occupancy load and accommodate substantially foreign employees. [CITE:3]

The statutory default “threshold number” is 1,000, unless the Minister has prescribed a lower number by notification in the Gazette. [CITE:3] Ex

sources.text: Licence needed to operate foreign employee dormitory, etc. 7.—(1) Unless exempted under section 32, a person must not operate any boarding premises as a foreign employee dormitory except under the authority of a valid licence for those premises. (2) Unless exempted under section 32, a proprietor of boarding premises must not use (or permit the use of) the premises as a foreign employee dormitory unless those premises are used as such by a licensed operator holding a valid licence relating to those premises. (3) A person who contravenes subsection (1) or (2) shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable on conviction — (a) to a fine not exceeding $500,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 2 years or to both; and (b) in the case of a second or subsequent conviction, to a fine not exceeding $1 million or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 4 years or to both. (4) It is a defence in proceedings for an offence under subsection (3) for contravening subsection (2) if the proprietor of boarding premises satisfies the court, on a balance of probabilities, that the proprietor did not know, and could not reasonably have been expected to know, that those premises were being used as a foreign employee dormitory otherwise than by the holder of a valid licence relating to those premises. question: Under the Metrication Act 1970, from what date does the International System of Units have legal force in Singapore?
answer: On and after 15 February 1971.
evidence_quote: On and after 15 February 1971, the use of the system of units known as the International System of Units has legal force and validity in Singapore
generated_answer:
As at 2026-11-06, the International System of Units (SI) has had legal force and validity in Singapore **on and after 15 February 1971** [CITE:1]. This is the date specified by section 3(1) of the Metrication Act 1970 [CITE:1].

Under section 2(1) of that Act, the "International System of Units" means the metric system of units set out in the First and Second Schedules, and includes the units in the Fourth Schedule unless the context is otherwise inconsistent; the abbreviation "SI" is also recognised as a legal reference to it [CITE:3]. The First Schedule sets out the six basic SI units (metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin and candela), the Second Schedule sets out the supplementary and derived units, and the Fourth Schedule covers units such as the hectare, tonne, litre and Celsius [CITE:12][CITE:7][CITE:4].

answer: The authorised betting operator pays it.
